items.title: Creating and Selling AI Coloring Books on Amazon KDP
items.hook: An episode of a series testing viral side hustles, made as paid Higgsfield promotion (#higgsfieldpartner). Its prompt is gated behind "comment Astra", and at KDP's real royalty the $10k/month coloring-book claim works out to about $3,660.
items.summary: An episode of a series testing viral money claims. The creator, a paid Higgsfield partner, shows a $9.99 kids' coloring book on Amazon, says to screenshot it into ChatGPT running GPT-6 Astra with the Higgsfield plugin plus a prompt, and repeats the claim that 33 sales a day make $10,000 a month. The prompt is never shown; it is offered to viewers who save, follow and comment "Astra". The tools exist as named and Higgsfield allows selling the output, but KDP pays about $3.69 a copy at $9.99 and allows only 2 new paperback titles a week.

note.spoken_transcript: Bro, you know that only 8% of people under the age of 21 have $10,000 to their name? Bro, if I was 21 again, I'd make $10,000 so easy. You know how? Amazon AI books, dude. People don't even know you can sell AI books on Amazon, $10 each AI book. 33 a day, what is that? I'll tell you, it's $330 a day. Now you multiply that by 30 days, what is that? I'll tell you again, it's 10k a month. Welcome back to Is He Onto Something or On Something, a series where I test viral side hustles to see if they actually work so you don't have to. Let's get it. Go to Amazon and then find a kids coloring book just like this. They're selling it for $9.99 and have sold over 12,000 units. Do the math, and that's a lot of money. So now take a screenshot of the listing, go to ChatGPT. Make sure you're using GPT-6 Astra, go to plugins, and connect the Higgsfield MCP plugin. Now paste in that screenshot with this exact prompt, and it'll give you a fully done coloring book ready to print. So it turns out Amazon handles all the printing and shipping of your books for you. So I guess he was onto something 'cause it is that easy. I'm gonna go upload 15 books. If you want the prompts that I used, then save this video, follow me, and comment the word Astra and I'll send it to you.

followup.answer_html:
Verdict: the tools are real, but the money is not. Every product the reel names exists under that name, and Higgsfield's terms allow you to sell the images. The income math is wrong. At $9.99, KDP pays the publisher about $3.69 a copy, not $10. So 33 sales a day nets about $3,657 a month, not the $9,900 the video claims. Hitting $10,000 would take about 90 sales a day, every day, before any costs. "I'm gonna go upload 15 books" also can't happen in one sitting: KDP lets you create only 2 new titles per format per week.

KDP economics

KDP's formula, from Paperback Royalty: royalty = (royalty rate x list price) - printing cost.

  1. Royalty rate on Amazon.com: 60% at a list price of $9.99 or more, 50% at $9.98 or less.
  2. Printing cost for black ink in the US, from Paperback Printing Cost: a flat $2.30 for 24 to 110 pages. Above 110 pages it is $1.00 plus $0.012 a page. A 30-, 60- or 100-page coloring book all cost $2.30 to print.
  3. Per copy at $9.99: (0.60 x $9.99) - $2.30 = $5.994 - $2.30 = $3.69.
  4. The video's math: 33 a day x $10 x 30 days = $9,900. KDP's math: 33 x 30 = 990 copies x $3.694 = $3,657 a month.
  5. To reach $10,000 a month at this price: $10,000 / 30 / $3.694 = about 90 copies a day.
  6. The on-screen Google sum, "$9.99 x 12,300 = $122,877", adds up list prices, not what the publisher is paid. At the real royalty, 12,300 copies pays about $45,400. The listing shows a publication date of May 22, 2024, so if the sales figure is true, that is roughly $1,600 a month over about 28 months. KDP does not publish per-book sales, so the 12,000-unit claim can't be checked.
  7. All of these are royalty figures before ad spend, returns, and the ChatGPT and Higgsfield subscriptions. The minimum list price at these page counts is $2.30 / 0.50 = $4.60 (Print Book Pricing), so the $9.99 price itself is allowed.

Tool chain, claim by claim

  1. "GPT-6 Astra": real. OpenAI's model list names GPT-6 Astra (gpt-6-astra) as its most capable current model. The reel only shows a browser tab titled "GPT-6 Astra: A new g...". It never shows ChatGPT's model picker.
  2. "Go to plugins": real. ChatGPT has a current feature called Plugins. Connectors were renamed "apps" in December 2025. The free ChatGPT plan can't connect apps (Connectors in ChatGPT), and the Plugins page gives no single plan cutoff. Only excerpts of these two OpenAI help pages could be read.
  3. "Higgsfield MCP plugin": real and official. Higgsfield publishes a Higgsfield Plugin for ChatGPT, also called Higgsfield MCP. To set it up, open ChatGPT's Plugins Directory, or go to higgsfield.ai/mcp and choose "Add Higgsfield plugin". Sign in to Higgsfield, authorize, then call it in chat with @Higgsfield (setup guide).
  4. Cost: a paid Higgsfield plan plus a paid ChatGPT plan. Higgsfield's help center says the plugin needs an "active paid subscription". The only free route is a 24-hour trial that turns into a billed Plus monthly plan unless you cancel it (Higgsfield blog). Higgsfield's pricing page builds its table with scripts, so plan prices could not be read from it. Third-party price lists contradict each other and are not used here.
  5. Selling the images: allowed. Higgsfield's Terms of Use say the company "does not claim ownership of any of your Inputs or Outputs, nor does it restrict your commercial use of Outputs". Its help center adds that this does not depend on your plan, but free-tier downloads may be watermarked. The catch: your uploads and outputs may be used to train Higgsfield's models unless you are on Enterprise or delete them. In this workflow, that includes the screenshot of someone else's bestselling book.

KDP rules the plan as filmed runs into

  1. AI disclosure. KDP's Content Guidelines require you to declare AI-generated text, images or translations when you publish, using a checkbox in the publishing flow. Pages generated from a prompt count as "AI-generated", not "AI-assisted".
  2. 2 new titles per format per week (Create a Book). Fifteen paperbacks take at least 8 weeks to create. KDP's own pages describe no exception process.
  3. Duplicate content. The Guide to Kindle Content Quality bars content "excessively reused, recycled, or repeated within or across books" and content "not significantly different from content in another book". The guide is written for Kindle ebooks, but it is KDP's clearest statement on near-duplicates. Fifteen books made from one prompt, each copying a bestseller, fit the pattern it describes.
  4. Disappointing or misleading books. The Content Guidelines disallow content "typically disappointing to customers" and descriptions that misrepresent the book.
  5. Rights. You must hold the publishing rights to what you upload (IP FAQ). KDP says nothing directly about generating pages from a screenshot of a competitor's book. The responsibility sits with the publisher, including for AI content.
  6. Not a low-content book. KDP's Low-Content Books page explicitly excludes coloring books, so the normal ISBN and distribution rules apply.

extra_sections.detail: The narration says "paste in that screenshot with this exact prompt", but the prompt text is not on screen in any of the 16 frames reviewed: [not shown]. The video cuts from a Higgsfield example page straight to a flipthrough video of a finished book. No ChatGPT chat window, model picker or plugin menu appears. What is legible: a browser tab reading "GPT-6 Astra: A new g[unreadable]"; a Higgsfield page with the subtitle "Every image an[unreadable] model"; and an Amazon listing showing Paperback $9.99, Spiral-bound $28.99, publication date May 22, 2024, and dimensions 8.5 x 0.2 x 8.5 inches. The word "plugin" is an editor's caption, not a menu label. The finished pages shown (unicorn with a birthday cake; sleeping unicorn under a moon) have clean black outlines but visible doubled, sketchy lines, and they appear as an MP4 flipthrough, not a print file. Nothing is known about what the prompt says, including any "outline styles" or "vector" settings.

extra_sections.heading: The gate and the sponsorship
extra_sections.detail: The prompt is withheld. To get it, the video says to save the video, follow the creator and comment the word "Astra", and the creator will send it, presumably by DM. It is not published anywhere, and delivery can't be verified. The caption carries #higgsfieldpartner and tags @higgsfield.ai, so the creator is paid by the vendor the video tells viewers to use. The creator's bio link appears to be a Higgsfield referral link to its MCP page; Instagram only returned it once, so treat this as lower confidence. Higgsfield's own free-to-start alternative is its AI Drawing Generator, which has an "AI Coloring" mode for "clean outlines, no shading" line art (higgsfield.ai/ai-drawing-generator). It is the same vendor. Gumroad and Etsy packs sold as "Higgsfield prompts" are not linked from Higgsfield or the creator.

extra_sections.heading: Portfolio project: ai-coloring-book-compiler (corrected)
extra_sections.detail:
A pipeline that generates themed line art, cleans it to pure black and white, and compiles a KDP-ready interior PDF. Stack: Python 3.11+, an image API (OpenAI, or Higgsfield's developer API at open.higgsfield.ai), OpenCV, ReportLab or PyMuPDF, and Pydantic. About 8 hours.
1. Generate structured JSON scene prompts for 20 or more pages, all in one theme.
2. Generate the images, threshold them to pure black and white, and clean up doubled lines. Keep them as raster images at 300 DPI minimum, with 600 DPI the recommended maximum to keep the file under 650 MB. Vectorizing with Potrace is optional, not required: KDP only asks for 300 DPI images embedded in the PDF.
3. Compile the PDF. Use an 8.5 x 11 in trim, or 8.5 x 8.5 like the filmed book; both are KDP sizes. Full-bleed art adds 0.125 in to the width and 0.25 in to the height, so the page becomes 8.625 x 11.25 or 8.625 x 8.75. Margins with bleed are at least 0.375 in on the outside and 0.375 in in the gutter for 24 to 110 pages. Embed fonts and images, flatten transparency, and use at least 7 pt text. Blank backs cost nothing extra, because any interior from 24 to 110 pages prints for the same $2.30.
4. Add a checker that rejects pages below 300 DPI, art inside the margin zone, or large filled black areas.
Out of scope: automating KDP uploads. Coloring books are not low-content books, and AI-generated pages must be declared at upload.

items.title: HeyGen HyperFrames: Open-Source Tool That Renders HTML to MP4 (Works With Claude Code, Codex, Cursor)
items.hook: An open-source framework that lets a coding agent write a video as HTML and render it to MP4, free and fully local, with a few HeyGen-hosted features priced separately.
items.summary: HeyGen has open-sourced HyperFrames, a framework that lets a coding agent write motion graphics as HTML and render them to MP4. It works with Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor, not only Claude. It ships 21 built-in skills, confirmed live in the repo as of 2026-09-28. The code is Apache 2.0 and local rendering is free and fully offline; HeyGen's own paid plans and credits only apply if you opt into HeyGen voice, avatar generation, or HeyGen's managed cloud rendering, and one built-in skill (changelog-video) requires a paid HeyGen account with no free fallback. GitHub stars: about 53.9k as of 2026-09-28 (the reel's 53.7K figure was close and dated to its own recording).

note.spoken_transcript: HeyGen just open-sourced a GitHub repo that turns Claude into a full-on motion designer, and it's completely free. It's called HyperFrames. It's already sitting at almost 54,000 stars on GitHub. The idea is simple: AI is already really good at writing HTML, so HyperFrames lets Claude write a video as HTML and then renders it straight into MP4. So you just tell Claude something like, 'Make me a 10-second product intro with a fade-in title, background video, and music.' It plans the video, builds the animations, adds the media, and renders the final file for you. It comes with 21 built-in skills, so it can make product launch videos, animated captions, beat-synced music videos, data visualizations, and even turn a GitHub pull request feature into an explainer video. You can pair it with Opus 5.5, and you basically have a motion design studio that works for free. Normally you'd need After Effects, a paid subscription, and hours of keyframing to get anything close to this. And because it's Apache 2.0 licensed, there are no render fees, and you can use it commercially. And to set it up, you can just open up Claude Code, ask it to install HyperFrames, and that's it. You're ready to start making and automating videos.

followup.answer_html:
HyperFrames is HeyGen's open-source framework (Apache 2.0) that lets an AI coding agent write a video as HTML and render it to MP4. It works with Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor as separate plugin surfaces, plus a standalone install path for any other agent, so Claude Code is one front end among several, not a requirement.

How it actually renders

Puppeteer drives headless Chrome to capture the HTML composition frame by frame, seeking to each exact frame rather than recording live playback, so a slow machine takes longer but produces the same output. FFmpeg then encodes the captured frames and mixes the audio into the final MP4.

Local rendering (npx hyperframes render) runs fully offline: no account, no API key, no network call needed. The only mark added is unsigned container metadata (renderer name and version), not a visible watermark, and it can be stripped with FFmpeg. There is no length cap on local output.

Sources: HyperFrames Introduction, rendering guide, both checked 2026-09-28.

What's free and where HeyGen charges

Two separate things:

  1. Self-hosted, local use. The code is Apache 2.0, verified directly in the repo's LICENSE file. Rendering locally costs nothing and needs no HeyGen account. Voice and music default to free local engines (Kokoro for voice, MusicGen for music) unless you specifically ask for HeyGen's versions. The only cost is your own machine's compute time.
  2. HeyGen's paid cloud and API. HeyGen's subscription plans, checked 2026-09-28 at heygen.com/pricing, run Free ($0, 3 videos/month), Creator ($29/mo), Pro ($49/mo), Business ($149/mo), and custom Enterprise, priced in credits. These only apply if you opt into a HeyGen-hosted feature: HeyGen voice or music, avatar generation, or HeyGen's own managed cloud rendering (a separate path from local rendering, where 4K renders are billed at 1.5x).

One built-in skill breaks the reel's "completely free" framing: changelog-video hardcodes a specific paid HeyGen voice and requires heygen auth login --oauth, with no local fallback documented. Running that one skill needs a HeyGen account and spends HeyGen credits. Avatar generation works the same way: it can prompt a HeyGen sign-in mid-session and then draws on your account's paid credit balance. Every other checked skill, including the beat-synced music video skill, uses free local defaults unless you deliberately sign in.

Built-in skills

21 skills, confirmed live in the repo's skills/ directory and independently on skills.sh, both checked 2026-09-28. That matches the reel's claim; it is not stale. The full list with what each one does is in the attached skills reference. Two things are easy to confuse with the 21 and are not part of it: a separate .agents/skills folder holds 6 small dev-only skills used only for the project's own changelog videos (changelog-video, the paid-voice one, lives here), and the docs "catalog" page lists 150+ prebuilt visual building blocks (carousels, chart styles, transitions) that are components, not agent skills.

Setting it up on Windows 11

Prerequisites: Node.js 22+ and FFmpeg, per the repo's README. PowerShell 5.1 has no &&, so each step below is its own line.

Standard package installs (ordinary winget packages, not HeyGen-specific and not from HeyGen's own docs):

winget install OpenJS.NodeJS
winget install Gyan.FFmpeg

Open a new PowerShell window so PATH updates take effect, then confirm:

node --version
ffmpeg -version

Install the plugin for Claude Code:

claude plugin marketplace add heygen-com/hyperframes
claude plugin install hyperframes@hyperframes

For Codex, Cursor, or any other agent, the standalone path from the same README works instead:

npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

First prompt that produces an actual MP4, from the official quickstart (swap in a real URL):

Using /hyperframes, make a 10-second product intro for https://example.com.

To remove it later:

claude plugin uninstall hyperframes@hyperframes

Gotchas

  • The changelog-video skill needs a paid HeyGen account and voice, and will not warn you first if an agent picks it.
  • Avatar generation can prompt a HeyGen sign-in mid-session and spends your paid credit balance.
  • HyperFrames' own "Cloud" rendering path (separate from local) needs a HeyGen account and API key, and 4K renders through it are billed at 1.5x.
  • No published render-time numbers exist for 1080p vs 4K on any hardware; you find out by testing on your own machine.
  • No Windows-specific setup guidance exists beyond "Node.js 22+, FFmpeg"; the winget commands above are standard packages, not HeyGen's own instructions.
  • Font licensing for the example and catalog templates (Bodoni Moda, Space Grotesk, Hanken, DM Mono, IBM Plex Mono, as seen in the reel) is undocumented anywhere in the project. Apache 2.0 covers the code, not necessarily the fonts, so verify font licensing separately before shipping a commercial video built from a catalog template.

Numbers, dated

GitHub stars: about 53.9k as of 2026-09-28 (the reel's on-screen "53.7K" and spoken "almost 54,000" were its own recording's figures and were already close, not wrong). Latest published version: 0.8.90 on npm as of 2026-09-28 (the reel's on-screen v0.8.82 is stale; the project ships frequent patch releases).

Bottom line

Install it if you want to render HTML compositions to MP4 locally for free, with any coding agent, not only Claude Code. Leave changelog-video and avatar-presenter alone unless you want a HeyGen account and are fine spending credits; everything else stays free and local by default.

items.title: Voicebox: a free, open-source, local voice-cloning and dictation app (GitHub: jamiepine/voicebox)
items.hook: A free open-source desktop app clones your voice from a few seconds of audio, then lets you dictate into any app with a global hotkey — no account, no subscription.
items.summary: A creator (on-screen "Nathan H." voice sample; posted as nathanhodgson.ai) pitches "Voicebox," an open-source desktop app (GitHub repo jamiepine/voicebox) that he calls a free alternative to the paid dictation app "Flow" (Wispr Flow, shown priced at $15/mo Pro). The reel intercuts talking-head shots of the creator with mocked-up screenshots of the app's landing page, its actual GitHub repo page, and its in-app UI: a voice-profile library, a "Clone voice" recording dialog, a global-hotkey dictation overlay that pastes text into apps like Notes, a text-to-speech generation panel with language and engine dropdowns, and an MCP server configuration that lets AI coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Cline) speak through a cloned voice profile via a `voicebox.speak()` call. Word-by-word burnt-in captions track the voiceover. The GitHub repo screenshot shows 19,785 stars (~19.8k), while an earlier marketing mockup of the same landing page shows "Star 55.4k" and a later caption reads "20000" — these three on-screen star figures do not match each other or the spoken/caption claim of "over 20,000." The language dropdown shows only the first 10 of the claimed 23 languages (cut off after Hebrew), and the engine dropdown shows only 3 of the claimed 7 engines (Qwen3-TTS, Qwen CustomVoice, LuxTTS). No Mac/Windows/Linux text or public URL appears on screen anywhere; the only URL visible is a local loopback address for the MCP server. The post ends with an Instagram comment-box mockup reading "Voice," matching the caption's gate: comment "VOICE" to be DMed the download link.

sections.heading: Frame 1 — Landing page mockup, creator intro
sections.detail: A browser-window mockup shows an app landing page: a redacted/blurred title bar and handle next to a mic icon, tabs "Clone" "Capture" with a "NEW" badge, and a star counter reading "Star 55.4k". Below, a gold vintage-microphone graphic, the tagline "THE OPEN-SOURCE AI VOICE STUDIO" and headline "Clone, dictate and create.", with a gold "DOWNLOAD" button and a "View on GitHub" button (GitHub octocat icon). Burnt-in caption word: "a". Cuts to the creator (young man, dark shirt, purple/orange-lit room, studio mic in frame) starting to speak.

sections.heading: Frame 2 — "Flow" branding stamped FREE over the same mockup
sections.detail: A "Flow" wordmark (with a small audio-bar icon) appears at top with an orange "FREE" stamp diagonally over it. note.spoken_transcript: Someone just made a free version of Whisperflow and it's already got over 20,000 stars on GitHub. It's called VoiceBox. It runs on your own computer so you don't need an account or a monthly plan. Give it a few seconds of your voice and it makes a copy and then you just hold down a key and talk and the words show up in any app that you're using. It works in 23 languages and comes with seven voice engines and it even has an MCP server so your AI agents can talk using your voice. So if you want to check it out, comment voice and I'll send you the link.

followup.answer_html:
Voicebox is a free, open-source desktop app that clones a voice from a short audio sample and does global-hotkey push-to-talk dictation, all on your own machine. Repository: jamiepine/voicebox. Official site: voicebox.sh.

The link the post withholds behind "comment VOICE" is https://voicebox.sh/ (same project as the GitHub repo). Identity is confirmed, not a guess: the reel's own GitHub screenshot, MCP config, and voicebox.speak() code line match the live repo and its docs exactly.

It is genuinely free (core app, MIT licence, no account needed) and genuinely local (no cloud fallback for cloning or dictation; models, voice data and captures stay on the machine).

Claim by claim (checked 2026-09-28)

Claim Verdict Detail
Over 20,000 GitHub stars Verified 55.9k stars today. The reel's own footage disagreed with itself: one "real" GitHub screenshot in the video showed 19,785 stars, under 20,000, while a separate marketing graphic in the same reel showed 55.4k. The claim holds now regardless of that mismatch.
7 local TTS engines Verified Qwen3-TTS, Qwen CustomVoice, LuxTTS, Chatterbox Multilingual, Chatterbox Turbo, HumeAI TADA, Kokoro.
23 languages Verified, with a caveat 23 is the maximum, reached only through one engine (Chatterbox Multilingual). Other engines cover fewer languages; two are English only.
MCP server so agents speak in your cloned voice Verified Built-in server at 127.0.0.1:17493/mcp, exposes voicebox.speak and related tools, with ready-made config for Claude Code, Cursor and Cline.
Mac, Windows and Linux builds False Prebuilt installers exist only for Mac (DMG) and Windows (MSI). Linux has no official build; it requires building from source or Docker.
No account or subscription Verified The core app is free forever with no account needed for local use. An optional paid cloud sync add-on ($12/yr or $48/yr) is listed as "coming soon" but is not required for cloning or dictation.

Install and first use

Mac

  1. Download the Apple Silicon or Intel DMG from voicebox.sh or the GitHub releases page.
  2. Install and open the app.
  3. Grant Microphone access when prompted (needed to record cloning samples and to dictate).
  4. Grant Accessibility and Input Monitoring access through the in-app link (needed for the hotkey to auto-paste into other apps; without it, dictation still transcribes into Voicebox's own Captures tab, it just won't paste elsewhere).
  5. Voices tab, New Voice, name it, then upload or record a 10-30 second sample.
  6. To dictate: hold the global hotkey, speak, release. The text auto-pastes into whatever field is focused.
  7. To generate speech: Generate tab, pick a voice profile, type text, Generate.

Windows

  1. Download the MSI installer from voicebox.sh or the GitHub releases page.
  2. Run it. The installer is currently unsigned, so Windows SmartScreen will warn it's unrecognized; click "Run anyway" to continue (the project says code signing is planned).
  3. Launch and grant microphone access when prompted.
  4. Same Voices, New Voice, Upload or Record steps as Mac.
  5. Same hotkey dictation flow as Mac, including auto-paste.

Caveats

  • Model sizes vary by engine, from Kokoro at 82M up to Qwen3-TTS at 1.7B and TADA at up to 3B. Plan disk space and VRAM around whichever engines you pick.
  • GPU support: Apple Silicon uses MLX/Metal, NVIDIA GPUs use CUDA, DirectML works on any Windows GPU, Intel Arc uses IPEX, AMD on Linux uses ROCm. CPU works everywhere but is slower. No specific RAM figure is published.
  • Licence: MIT, no non-commercial restriction.
  • Watermarking: none found in the README or docs. Cloned-voice output carries no built-in disclosure marker.
  • Permissions: microphone on both platforms; on Mac, Accessibility and Input Monitoring for the hotkey to auto-paste; on Windows, expect a SmartScreen warning since the installer is not code-signed yet.
  • Optional paid tiers ($12/yr cloud backup, $48/yr studio) are listed as "coming soon" and are not required for local cloning or dictation.

What you're choosing between

Wispr Flow, the paid tool the reel pitches Voicebox as a free replacement for, is cloud-only: transcription always happens on Wispr's servers, never on-device. Free tier caps at 2,000 words/week on desktop. Pro is $15/mo ($12/mo billed annually). Growth is $23/mo per user ($18/mo annual). Enterprise is custom priced.

Other maintained local, open-source options:

  • Handy: dictation only, no voice cloning. Official builds for Mac, Windows and Linux, MIT licence, most recently updated of the group (September 2026).
  • VoiceInk: dictation only, Mac only. Source is GPLv3, but the compiled app needs a paid licence for auto-updates and support unless you build it yourself.
  • Chatterbox: voice cloning and TTS, but a library, not a packaged app. MIT, Linux and Mac, GPU recommended.
  • OpenVoice: voice cloning and TTS library, MIT, free for commercial use, but its last commit was over a year ago, the least actively maintained of the group.

If you want one app that does cloning, dictation and MCP together, Voicebox is the only match among these, with the Linux caveat above. If you only want dictation with an official Linux build, Handy is the more complete option there.
followup.next_action: Filed in To Watch > Concept Explainers with the other Jarvis-style assistant reels, per the only instruction on this item. To try the tool itself, download from voicebox.sh (Mac and Windows only for now; Linux needs building from source).

items.title: AI kids' coloring books on Amazon KDP, made with EveryGen inside Claude
items.hook: The reel promises '60% royalties'. At its own $6.99 price KDP pays 50% minus a $2.84 print cost: 66 cents a copy.
items.summary: A sponsored reel (#everygenpartner) shows how to connect EveryGen to Claude as a custom connector at everygen.ai/api/mcp, generate a kids' coloring book (the demo theme is fairies and garden gnomes), and upload it as an 8.5 x 11 paperback on Amazon KDP. It points to the 'Hopscotch Girls' coloring book at $6.99 as 'sold over 34,000 copies', but the screen shows that 34,195 is the book's rating count, which a calculator then multiplies by the price. It ends with a comment gate: comment 'Claude' for a free guide. The workflow is real. The earnings pitch is not: the 60% rate starts at $9.99, printing costs $2.84 a copy, AI use must be disclosed, KDP now allows only 2 new titles per format per week, EveryGen has no free plan, and it only makes images, not a print-ready book.

sections.heading: a
sections.detail: b

note.spoken_transcript: test

followup.answer_html:
Verdict

  • Is it real? Yes. Amazon KDP accepts coloring books made with AI images, as long as you disclose the AI use when you upload (KDP Content Guidelines). Amazon prints each copy when it is ordered and ships it, so you hold no stock.
  • Is it free? KDP itself is: no sign-up, listing or monthly fee (Start publishing with KDP). EveryGen, the tool in the reel, is not. It has no free plan, and the cheapest plan is $14 a month billed annually, which is $168 paid up front (EveryGen pricing).
  • Can it be made free? Yes, with no cash cost: Adobe Firefly's free coloring-page generator or Stable Diffusion on your own PC for the art, GIMP to clean it up, Scribus for layout and the PDF, and KDP's own Cover Creator for the cover. The catches: Adobe does not publish its free daily limit, and local Stable Diffusion needs a capable graphics card.
  • What a copy actually pays: far less than the reel suggests. See below.

What a $6.99 copy pays

KDP's formula is royalty = (rate x list price) - printing cost (Paperback Royalty). The rate is 50% up to $9.98 and 60% only from $9.99. So the reel's "60% royalties" does not apply at its own $6.99 price.

For the book the reel shows (8.5 x 11 in, black ink, white paper), Amazon.com charges a flat $2.84 to print any book from 24 to 110 pages (Printing Cost). So 60, 80 or 100 pages all cost the same.

  1. At $6.99: 0.50 x 6.99 = $3.495, minus $2.84 = $0.66 per copy. Not the $4.19 that "60% of $6.99" suggests. You need 153 sales to earn $100.
  2. At $9.99: 0.60 x 9.99 = $5.99, minus $2.84 = $3.15 per copy. Moving the price from $9.98 to $9.99 is worth about a dollar a copy.
  3. The lowest price KDP accepts for this book is $2.84 / 0.50 = $5.68.
  4. UK at GBP 6.99 pays about GBP 1.35 (print cost GBP 2.15). EU at EUR 6.99 pays about EUR 1.02 (print cost EUR 2.48). Using the same 6.99 figure in each currency is an assumption made for comparison.

The "34,000 copies sold" line is not a sales figure. The reel's own frame shows the Amazon page reading "4.8 stars (34,195)". That is the number of ratings. The next frame shows a calculator doing 34195 x 6.99 = 239,023, which multiplies ratings by the full shelf price. Amazon publishes no one's sales counts. Even if every rating were a sale, a book with these specs would have paid its publisher about $22,400, not $239,000. The book shown is also part of a 10-book series from "a small business brand", not something made in minutes with an AI tool.

What Amazon requires if you do it

  1. The AI disclosure. Content counts as AI-generated if an AI tool made the first version, even if you edit it heavily afterwards. You must say so at upload. Shoppers never see the answer. KDP acts on books that fail to disclose, not on books that use AI (Content Guidelines).
  2. Rights and trademarks. You must hold the rights to everything you upload. Uploading content you have no rights to can get the book removed, cost you royalties and hurt your account (Intellectual Property FAQ). Titles and keywords may not use trademarked names, other authors or books, "bestseller" or "free" (Metadata Guidelines).
  3. Quality. Serious defects take a book off sale until fixed. KDP says continuing to add problem content "could affect your account status, up to and including termination" (Content Quality Guide). For AI pages that means no fake lettering, broken lines or mangled hands.
  4. Publishing limits. Since 21 September 2026, KDP allows only 2 new titles per format per week, resetting Sunday 00:00 UTC (Paperback Submission Guidelines, Publishers Lunch). The limit was 3 a day in 2023, then 10 per format per week.
  5. Tax. Every publisher completes a tax interview. If you live outside the US and skip it or get it wrong, 30% of US royalties is withheld (Tax Withholding).
  6. Two boxes to leave unticked. "Low-content book" (KDP says coloring books generally are not, and ticking it loses the free ISBN) and Expanded Distribution (coloring books are explicitly excluded) (Low-Content Books, Expanded Distribution).

What the reel overstates or leaves out

  1. The 60% rate and the print cost, as above.
  2. The sales figure, which is a ratings count.
  3. "A coloring book ready to go in a few minutes." EveryGen makes single images. None of its public pages mention page layout, trim size, bleed or PDF export. Turning the images into a KDP-ready file is most of a day's work.
  4. No copyright. In the US, purely AI-generated images cannot be copyrighted (U.S. Copyright Office, Federal Register guidance). You can still sell them, but anyone can copy your pages and sell them too.
  5. Competition. Generic kids' coloring themes are described as saturated, even by companies selling tools into this niche. No independent earnings data for coloring books exists. Every niche income figure found came from people selling tools or courses. The nearest independent figure covers all self-published authors: a median of $12,749 a year, with about a quarter earning $0 to $1,000 (ALLi survey).
  6. Payment lag. KDP pays about 60 days after the end of the month of the sale (Payment Thresholds).
  7. The sponsorship. The caption carries #everygenpartner, so the creator is promoting EveryGen as a partner.

EveryGen against the free path

  • The connector is real, and the reel's setup matches EveryGen's own page: in Claude, go to Customize > Connectors > Add custom connector, and paste https://everygen.ai/api/mcp (EveryGen MCP). Claude's free plan allows one custom connector (Claude help).
  • Plans (billed annually): Basic $14/month ($168 a year) for 200 credits; Professional $19/month ($228) for 350; Creator $49/month ($588) for 800. Month to month: $29.99 for Professional and $69.99 for Creator. A $19.99 month-to-month price for Basic was read once but did not show on a recheck. Credits do not roll over.
  • What one book costs in credits: about 4 credits per "Nano Banana Pro" image, going by the page's own ratios. A 62-page book with 30 designs printed on one side, a cover and about 9 retries is roughly 40 images, or 160 credits. That fits the Basic plan. The reel's own screen appears to show 13 credits for six images, so some models cost less. EveryGen does not publish a price per model.
  • The commercial-use line on the pricing page names videos only ("You can monetize videos made with Everygen without any restrictions"). It says nothing about images in printed books. Check the terms before publishing.
  • The free path: Adobe Firefly coloring pages allows use "in published coloring books" under Adobe's guidelines. ComfyUI runs Stable Diffusion locally. The original Stable Diffusion license claims no rights in your output. Then GIMP for cleanup, Scribus for layout and PDF export, and KDP's Cover Calculator or Cover Creator for the cover.
  • One trap: Colorin AI gives 8 free pages, but they may not be sold. Its commercial license starts at $11.99 a month.

Where the adjacent platforms fit

The same 30 cleaned pages can also be sold as a printable PDF.

  1. Gumroad: free and live in minutes. It takes 10% + $0.50 on direct sales and 30% on Discover sales (pricing). AI-made products are allowed (prohibited list). This is the best first add-on.
  2. Etsy: buyers already search there for printables. Fees are $0.20 per listing, 6.5% per transaction and about 3% + $0.25 for card processing, and some new sellers pay a one-time setup fee of about $15. AI use must be disclosed. Etsy's own pages blocked automated reading, so these figures come from seller guides (Craftybase).
  3. Payhip: free plan with a 5% fee, but no marketplace traffic of its own.
  4. Teachers Pay Teachers: $29 to join, and you keep 55% on the Basic plan.
  5. Lulu: a second print outlet. Lulu keeps 20% of print sales on its own store (revenue guide).
  6. Redbubble, TeePublic and Amazon Merch on Demand: for shirts and merchandise, not coloring pages. Merch needs an approval that guides say takes 2 to 12 weeks.
  7. IngramSpark: prohibits AI-generated content outright (catalog integrity rules). Do not use it for this book.
  8. Draft2Digital: rejects fully AI-generated content that has not been extensively edited (FAQ).
  9. Canva Creators: needs a portfolio application with a review of up to about 2 months.

The attached day-one guide turns all of this into 9 timed blocks, about 10 hours from an empty KDP account to a submitted 62-page book. It gives exact settings for each block, a never-do list, and step-by-step Gumroad and Etsy setup for the following week.

Not confirmed

  • Adobe Firefly's free daily generation count, output size and watermark policy.
  • EveryGen's image output size, credit cost per model, top-up prices, and whether its commercial-use terms cover images in print.
  • The exact wording of KDP's AI-disclosure answer options, which come from a third-party guide, and a few KDP button labels.
  • Etsy, Redbubble, Payhip, TeePublic and Canva figures, which come from secondary sources because their own pages blocked reading.
  • IngramSpark's payout terms.
  • The prices of a Bowker ISBN, Adobe's paid plans and proof-copy shipping.
  • The example book's real sales.

extra_sections.heading: What the reel says
extra_sections.detail: Connect EveryGen to Claude as a custom connector, ask it for a kids' coloring book (the demo uses fairies and garden gnomes), and within minutes you have a cover and pages. Upload them to Amazon KDP, where Amazon prints and ships each copy worldwide and you 'collect 60% royalties'. As proof it points to a $6.99 coloring book that it says has 'sold over 34,000 copies'. The caption says '20 minutes a day and some consistency is all you need' and is tagged #everygenpartner, marking it as sponsored.

extra_sections.heading: How KDP pays
extra_sections.detail: Paperback royalty = (rate x list price) - printing cost. The rate is 50% up to $9.98 (GBP 7.98, EUR 9.98) and 60% from $9.99 (GBP 7.99, EUR 9.99). An 8.5 x 11 in black-and-white book on white paper costs a flat $2.84 to print on Amazon.com for 24 to 110 pages (GBP 2.15 in the UK, EUR 2.48 in the EU). Above 110 pages it is $1.00 + $0.017 per page. At $6.99 you get $0.66 a copy; at $9.99, $3.15. There are no upfront fees, and the free KDP ISBN works only for KDP printing. Direct deposit has no minimum, and payment arrives about 60 days after the end of the month of the sale. Review takes up to 72 hours on Amazon.com and up to 5 days elsewhere, plus up to 72 more hours before the book shows in search. Proof copies cost the printing cost plus shipping.

extra_sections.heading: The free toolchain
extra_sections.detail:
1. Art: Adobe Firefly's coloring-page generator on a free Adobe account (commercial use in published coloring books is allowed under Adobe's Generative AI User Guidelines; the daily limit is not published), or Stable Diffusion run locally through ComfyUI or AUTOMATIC1111 (needs a capable graphics card).
2. Cleanup: GIMP. Convert to grayscale, scale to 2250 x 3000 px at 300 ppi, apply Threshold for pure black and white, then Despeckle.
3. Layout: Scribus, on Letter-size 8.5 x 11 pages with 0.5 in margins, no bleed, and a 'test your colors' box on the back of each design so no page is blank. Export the PDF with fonts embedded and no printer marks.
4. Cover: KDP Cover Creator, which is free inside KDP, or your own PDF built on the KDP Cover Calculator template.
Colorin AI's 8 free pages may not be sold.

extra_sections.heading: Rules and risks
extra_sections.detail:
1. Disclose AI-generated text and images at upload.
2. No trademarked names, other authors, 'bestseller' or 'free' in titles or keywords, and no misleading categories.
3. Hold the rights to every image you upload.
4. Quality defects can pull a book from sale, and repeated problem content can lead to account termination.
5. KDP allows 2 new titles per format per week since 21 September 2026.
6. Purely AI-generated images have no US copyright, so competitors can copy your pages.
7. Non-US publishers who skip the tax interview have 30% of US royalties withheld.
8. Coloring books cannot use Expanded Distribution.
9. Enrolling an ebook in KDP Select requires digital exclusivity to Amazon.
10. IngramSpark bans AI-generated content.

extra_sections.heading: Similar platforms
extra_sections.detail:
1. Gumroad: free, 10% + $0.50 per direct sale, AI-made products allowed.
2. Etsy digital downloads: $0.20 per listing, 6.5% per transaction plus card processing, AI use must be disclosed, crowded.
3. Payhip: free plan with a 5% fee, no marketplace traffic.
4. Teachers Pay Teachers: $29 to join, you keep 55%.
5. Lulu: keeps 20% of print sales on its own store.
6. Redbubble and TeePublic: merchandise, tier-based fees or fixed payouts.
7. Amazon Merch on Demand: approval reportedly takes 2 to 12 weeks, royalty tiers since June 2026.
8. Draft2Digital: $20 activation fee, rejects unedited AI content.
9. IngramSpark: bans AI content.

items.hook: One actor plays the interviewer and both candidates to run the same four RAG interview questions twice, laying out exactly where a textbook answer stops and a production engineer's answer begins.
items.summary: A single creator (bashi_fuirkashi) plays all three roles in a scripted "AI Engineer Interview (RAG Edition)" skit, cutting between a black-jacket interviewer, a "🧠 Theory" candidate, and a "🖥️ Builder" candidate who are asked the same four questions. (1) How would you build a RAG pipeline in production: Theory recites the basic ingest-chunk-embed-store-retrieve-generate loop (shown as a simple 5-step Query→Embedding model→Vector DB→Retrieved contexts→LLM→Response diagram); Builder says he'd start from data and retrieval requirements first, then build ingestion, chunking, embedding, indexing, retrieval, re-ranking, generation and evaluation as separately measurable components — illustrated on screen by a far more elaborate "Enterprise Knowledge Management with RAG" data-flow diagram with real-time ingestion, CDC, vector upserts and a grounded-answer output. (2) Users are getting confident-but-wrong answers: Theory would tweak the prompt and retrieve more chunks; Builder first determines whether it's a retrieval or generation failure by logging queries, retrieval scores, context and responses, then fixes chunking/metadata filters/hybrid search/query rewriting/re-ranking if retrieval is bad, or the prompt/citations/forced abstention if generation is bad. (3) Traffic jumps 10x, latency and cost spike: Theory suggests a faster model plus caching; Builder says he'd profile each pipeline stage (embedding, vector search, re-ranking, generation each have different latency profiles), cache repeated queries/retrieval, batch embeddings at ingestion, trim unnecessary context, parallelize retrieval calls, and route simpler requests to what the audio garbles into "re-remodels." (4) Could you build this right now: Theory would need to look up the implementation; Builder says he's already built one and offers to pull up the repo, and is hired on the spot. The skit ends with the hired "Builder" crediting an AI engineering community — shown on screen as a screen-recording of a community feed with a post from "Kitu Komya" about an AMA call and a roadmap screenshot — for a learning roadmap, resume projects, and daily calls with working engineers, then pitches viewers to comment a keyword to get it sent to them, capped by a "You're hired" / "I hate you" exchange.

note.spoken_transcript: Same question to you both. How would you build a RAG pipeline in a production environment? This is going to be easy. Well, first you ingest your documents, chunk them, create embeddings, store them in a vector database, retrieve relevant chunks, then pass them into an LLM to generate the answer. Same foundation, but in production, I'd start with the data and retrieval requirements first. What documents are we indexing? How frequently do they change? What queries are users making? Then I'd build ingestion, chunking, embedding, indexing, retrieval, re-ranking, generation, and evaluation as separate components so I can measure and improve each one independently. Now the users are complaining that the RAG system keeps giving confident answers with the wrong information. What would you do? I'd improve the prompt and maybe increase the number of chunks we retrieve. Well, first I'd figure out whether it's a retrieval failure or a generation failure. I'd log the query, retrieve documents, relevant scores, context sent to the model, and the final response. If the retrieval is bad, I might change chunking and add metadata filters, hybrid search, query rewriting, or re-ranking. If retrieval is good, but the generated answer is bad, then I'd work on the generation prompt, citations, or force the model to abstain when the context doesn't support an answer. All right, traffic just went up by 10x. Now latency and costs are killing us. Use a faster model and cache the responses. Possibly, but I'd profile the pipeline first. Embedding, vector search, re-ranking, and generation all have different latency profiles. I'd cache repeated queries or retrieval results, batch embeddings during ingestion, limit unnecessary context, run independent retrieval calls in parallel, and route simpler requests, and re-remodels. If I gave you our documents and API access right now, could you build this? I'd probably need to look up implementation first. I've actually already built one. I can pull up the repo and show you. You're hired. Where'd you learn all this? Thanks. I joined this AI engineering community. They have a full learning roadmap, projects to put on my resume, and daily calls with working AI and machine learning engineers. If you want to join, comment interview, I'll send it to you. I hate you.

followup.answer_html:
What it is

A scripted two-candidate interview skit. One creator (bashi_fuirkashi) plays all three parts: an unlabeled interviewer, a candidate labeled "Theory," and a candidate labeled "Builder." Both candidates get the same four RAG interview questions back to back. The Builder is hired on the spot, credits an AI engineering community for what he knows, and the reel ends with a pitch to comment "Interview" to get sent that community.

On screen

  • Title cards: "Theory vs Builder" and "AI Engineer Interview (RAG Edition)"
  • Speaker labels run through the whole reel: Theory (short-sleeve shirt), Builder (long-sleeve shirt); the interviewer (black jacket) has no label
  • Theory's pipeline answer is illustrated with a simple 5-step diagram: Query -> Embedding model -> Vector DB -> Retrieved contexts -> LLM -> Response
  • Builder's pipeline answer is illustrated with a more elaborate 7-stage "Enterprise Knowledge Management with RAG" diagram: knowledge sources, real-time ingestion/CDC, embedding generation, vector database, user query, retrieval and generation, grounded answer
  • The closing frame overlays a screen recording of a community feed. The group header is small and blurred but reads approximately "BASWE AI Engineer." Visible in it: a post by "Kitu Komya" (an AMA covering AI vs ML roles, careers, project choice, and interview prep, crediting someone named Christopher with a job tracker he built using Claude Cowork and MCPs), plus fragments of other posts (a Leetcode note, a system design note, a recruiter-call note)
  • No price, handle, or URL for the comment-gated offer appears anywhere in the frames or the caption

Side by side: the four questions

Question Theory answer Production answer
How would you build a RAG pipeline in production? Ingest documents, chunk them, embed, store in a vector DB, retrieve, pass to an LLM. One pipe. Start from the data and query requirements first (what's indexed, how often it changes, what people actually ask), then build ingestion, chunking, embedding, indexing, retrieval, re-ranking, generation, and evaluation as separate components so each can be measured and improved on its own.
Users are getting confident answers that are wrong. What do you do? Improve the prompt, retrieve more chunks. Work out first whether it's a retrieval failure or a generation failure: log the query, the retrieved docs and their relevance scores, the context actually sent to the model, and the final response. If retrieval is bad: fix chunking, add metadata filters, hybrid search, query rewriting, re-ranking. If generation is bad: work the prompt, add citations, force the model to abstain when the context doesn't support an answer.
Traffic just went up 10x, latency and cost are climbing. Use a faster model and cache the responses. Profile the pipeline first, since embedding, vector search, re-ranking, and generation each have a different latency profile. Then: cache repeated queries or retrieval results, batch embeddings at ingestion time, trim unnecessary context, run retrieval calls in parallel, and route simpler requests to smaller, cheaper models.
Could you build this right now with our documents and API access? Would need to look up the implementation first. Already built one, offers to pull up the repo. Hired on the spot.

Checked against documentation

  • Exchange 1's component-by-component pipeline matches how the frameworks themselves describe RAG: LlamaIndex's own intro lists loading, indexing, storing, querying, and evaluation as five separate stages built and measured independently: Introduction to RAG - LlamaIndex
  • Exchange 2's retrieval fixes are real, named techniques with primary docs: Hybrid Search - Pinecone, Hybrid Search Explained - Weaviate, Filter by metadata - Pinecone, Filters - Weaviate, Query Transformations - LangChain, Rerank overview - Cohere
  • Exchange 2's generation fixes (citations, forced abstention) match Anthropic's own guardrail guidance: Reduce hallucinations - Claude docs, Citations - Claude docs. The retrieval-vs-generation split is also how the Ragas evaluation framework scores RAG systems: Ragas available metrics
  • Exchange 3's fixes each have a working primary source: Redis semantic cache, OpenAI Batch API (batch embeddings run at 50% cost with a separate rate limit pool, slower turnaround), RouteLLM (routes simple requests to a cheaper model, reports up to 85% cost cut while keeping about 95% of the stronger model's benchmark score). "Trim unnecessary context" and "parallelize retrieval calls" are real engineering practices but not distinct products with their own docs, so no link is given for those two specifically.

What I'd push back on

  • "Retrieve more chunks" (Theory's fix in exchange 2) is not reliably better. The Lost in the Middle study found model accuracy drops when the relevant passage sits in the middle of a long context rather than at the start or end, and later work found more retrieved passages can hurt once irrelevant ones are mixed in. What matters is whether the added chunks are actually relevant and where the right one lands, not the count. Lost in the Middle (arXiv 2307.03172)
  • Re-ranking (named as a retrieval fix) adds real latency and per-query cost. It's worth it when a wrong answer costs more than the delay; worth skipping, or using a lighter model, when the product has a tight response-time budget or retrieval is already precise.
  • Caching repeated queries or retrieval results (named as a cost fix) goes stale if the underlying documents change. Redis's own docs flag this directly: cached answers need scoping and a TTL so they stay aligned with the knowledge base, otherwise a cache hit can return a confidently wrong, outdated answer, which is the exact failure the reel spends exchange 2 on.
  • Forcing the model to abstain when context doesn't support an answer (named as a generation fix) trades recall for precision. It cuts false answers but also makes the model decline some questions it could have answered from a partial context. Which way to lean depends on whether a wrong confident answer or an unnecessary "I don't know" costs more for the use case.

The comment gate

Commenting "Interview" leads into BASWE.Ai, a real program run by Bashiri Smith. The reel's creator account links to it directly from its own Instagram bio.

There are three tiers:

  • A free Skool community, "Become an AI Engineer" (about 6,600 members): starter roadmaps and networking, positioned as the entry point into the paid tier.
  • A paid Skool community, "BASWE.Ai Engineer" (281 members, $89/month, price stated to rise once membership passes 500, 7-day refund window): daily coaching calls with engineers and recruiters, a learning roadmap covering LLMs/RAG/agents, a portfolio project system, resume and LinkedIn review, mock interviews, job-search support. This matches what the hired candidate describes in the script.
  • A separate, higher-priced coaching offer at baswe.ai, built around a guarantee (refund plus $10,000 if you don't land a higher-paying role) and a claimed average of 176 days to an offer. Its actual price is not published anywhere reachable; the only path is "book a call," a standard high-ticket sales pattern. Treat this tier's cost as unknown, not as free or as $89.

No independent reviews turned up on Reddit or Trustpilot, so the program's growth and salary claims rest on its own marketing. The reel itself is a scripted, staged testimonial built to drive comments into a DM funnel, not an organic recommendation.

items.summary: A talking-head reel by @vee_daily19 says Outlier, Mercor, Alignerr, Surge AI and 25+ other companies hire through resume screens, take-home tasks or portfolio reviews instead of interviews. It offers the full list and a resume template to anyone who comments "TECH". Seven companies appear on screen, as logos or in a scrolled reference document: Outlier, Mercor, Alignerr, Surge AI, DataAnnotation.tech, Clickworker/UHRS and Invisible Technologies. All are AI-training or microtask platforms that take on contractors. Most screen with an ID check plus a skills assessment, and Mercor and some Alignerr roles add an AI-run interview. None has an application deadline. The creator published a free 41-company version of the list on Substack the same day.

followup.answer_html:
The reel names 7 companies. The "25+" in the caption is never shown in the video. The PDF, Tech Companies That Hire Without a Traditional Interview, covers all 7. For each one it gives the apply link, the actual hiring process, roles and eligibility, pay, deadline and red flags.

  1. Outlier (by Scale AI): outlier.ai. Profile, ID check, then an assessment for each project.
  2. Mercor: mercor.com/experts. Resume plus an AI-run interview of about 20 minutes. Mercor says its average contracted rate is $110/hr.
  3. Alignerr (by Labelbox): alignerr.com. ID check, and some roles add an AI interview. It states an average of about $80/hr.
  4. Surge AI: consultant network. A paid assessment, then $60/hr. The credential-only expert roles are on a separate workforce page.
  5. DataAnnotation.tech: dataannotation.tech. An unpaid starter assessment. The site states $25-150+/hr depending on the role.
  6. Clickworker / UHRS: sign-up form. Qualification tests for each task type. Pay per task is low.
  7. Invisible Technologies: Meridial freelance board. A form plus a skills assessment. Postings pay $8-65/hr.

What could not be confirmed:

  • No deadlines. None of the 7 has an application deadline. All take applications on a rolling basis.
  • Pay figures. Some come from the company itself and some are only reported. Clickworker publishes no rates at all, and the reel's own figures don't always match the companies' pages. The PDF marks which is which.
  • Role listings. The Mercor and Outlier job dashboards only load in a browser, so the specific roles and rates there could not be checked.
  • "No interview" is only partly true. Every platform still screens applicants, sometimes with an AI interview. All 7 hire gig workers as contractors. Deactivation without explanation is the most common complaint.

The longer list the reel offers by DM is already free on the creator's Substack: 25 tech companies hiring without traditional interviews. It names 41 companies with apply links. The 34 beyond these 7 were not checked.

extra_sections.heading: The companies and where to apply
extra_sections.detail:
1. Outlier (Scale AI): outlier.ai. Profile, Persona ID check, then a paid or unpaid assessment for each project. Needs at least an associate degree, a local phone number and an ID. Pay is set per project and paid weekly; the reel's figures ($15-180/hr) are reported. Rolling.
2. Mercor: mercor.com/experts. Resume plus an AI-run interview of about 20 minutes (up to 3 attempts). About 140+ supported countries. Official average contracted rate is $110/hr, paid weekly. Rolling. Many applicants report sitting in the talent pool with no work.
3. Alignerr (Labelbox): alignerr.com. Google sign-in, resume, ID check, and for some roles a 15-20 minute AI interview or a domain assessment. Official pay averages about $80/hr (range $30-120). Rolling. Some workers report deactivations over back pay.
4. Surge AI: the consultant network (Finance, Accounting, Healthcare Ops, Coding) pays $100 for the assessment, $100 more if accepted, then $60/hr. Expert roles need top credentials, pay e.g. $200-400/hr, and you apply by emailing talent@surgehq.ai. Staff jobs are at surgehq.ai/careers. Rolling. A 2025 class action alleges it misclassified annotators as contractors.
5. DataAnnotation.tech (owned by Surge AI): unpaid starter assessment, then task access. The site states $40-150+/hr for specialized work and $25-40/hr for language roles. Rolling. There are reports of unexplained account cancellations.
6. Clickworker / UHRS: sign-up form, a profile quiz, then qualification tests for each task type. UHRS belongs to Microsoft and is reached through Clickworker. No official rates; reported pay is about $2-9/hr. Trustpilot score is 2.4/5. Rolling.
7. Invisible Technologies: trainer roles are on the Meridial Greenhouse board, applied for with a form and skills assessment. Postings pay $8-65/hr. Many roles are limited to one country or language. Rolling. Some reviews describe unpaid assessments and deactivations.

extra_sections.heading: How no-interview AI-data hiring actually works
extra_sections.detail: You create a profile instead of going through a recruiter screen. Then you pass a qualification step instead of a live interview: a skills test, a paid or unpaid starter task, a portfolio review, or an AI-run interview. Passing gets you into a task queue or talent pool, not a job. Almost everyone works as an independent contractor with no benefits. What to watch: country and ID rules that can block you after unpaid work; unexplained account deactivation, which is the most common complaint across these platforms; queues that dry up without warning; and unpaid assessment hours. Treat this as side income, and check who owns the platform.

items.title: Ranking of Seven AI Certifications by Hiring Value, S to D
items.hook: Only three of the seven rank A or S. None of the three is free, and the top Anthropic credential is currently closed to anyone without a partner-company email.
items.summary: An Instagram reel ranks seven AI certificates by how much they help you get hired. The tier board on screen matches the narration. S tier: Claude Certified Architect (Anthropic; proctored, technical, covers agentic systems and MCP) and Generative AI with Large Language Models (DeepLearning.AI + AWS; strong LLM fundamentals). A tier: Google AI Essentials (beginner-friendly, an introduction to prompting). B tier: HubSpot AI for Marketing (useful for marketers, too niche for others). C tier: Career Essentials in Generative AI by Microsoft and LinkedIn (easy but proves little). D tier: Ultimate AI Course Bundle (no standard curriculum or recognized credential) and IBM AI Engineering (useful content, but 3-6 months for limited hiring value). The reel held back its links for people who commented; the answer here supplies them for the A and S tiers. What the research found: Claude Certified Architect - Foundations is a real $125 proctored exam, but registration needs an email at a Claude Partner Network company. Generative AI with LLMs is a paid Coursera certificate of about 17-20 hours whose exact price is not shown until checkout. Google AI Essentials costs $49/month after a 7-day free trial and takes about 4-8 hours.

note.spoken_transcript: Most AI certificates look good on your LinkedIn but they do almost nothing for your career. So let me give you an honest ranking and tell you exactly which certificates you need to get hired. Microsoft plus LinkedIn Generative AI, this is C tier. Easy and polished but it does not prove real skills. Claude Certified Architect, S tier. So it's proctored, technical and focused on agentic systems and MCB. And it's one of the strongest AI credentials right now. Google AI Essentials, A tier. It's beginner-friendly, Google-backed and a solid introduction to prompt engineering. HubSpot AI for Marketing, B tier. Useful for marketers and creators but too niche for everyone else. Generative AI with LLMs by Deep Learning AI and AWS, S tier. Strong LLM fundamentals and much more better than another basic prompting course. Ultimate AI Course Bundle, D tier. No standard curriculum or recognized credentials, you can just skip it. IBM AI Engineering Certificate, D tier. Useful content but it takes 3-6 months to complete it which is too much of time for a credential with limited hiring value. So your best path depends upon whether you're an engineer, an entrepreneur or starting from scratch. So come in certificate, I'll send you the form. Full roadmap and do not forget to follow me. Bye.

What "MCB" refers to in the spoken line "focused on agentic systems and MCB" — likely a mishearing of "MCP" (Model Context Protocol), but no on-screen text confirms this.
Exact characters of the two verify URLs shown in tiny print (skilljar.com/c/4dbjr6apfgpd and coursera.org/verify/4ROJ4I4QXZWL) could not be confirmed with full pixel-level certainty.

Full names of the recipients on the IBM AI Engineering certificate (frame 1/13) and the first name preceding "Nandkumar Dhondkar" on the AWS/DeepLearning.AI certificate (frame 9) are partly illegible/obscured.

followup.answer_html:
None of the three certificates is free. You can learn some of the material for free, but you pay for the certificate itself every time.

  1. Claude Certified Architect - Foundations (Anthropic), S tier

    • Link: registration page. Also see the certification FAQ.
    • Cost: the exam is $125. The prep courses are free, but they do not give you the credential. Each retake costs the full $125 again. Renewal after 12 months is free.
    • Catch: registration needs an email address at a company in the Claude Partner Network. Anthropic's FAQ says "personal email addresses will not work." Unless your employer is a partner, you cannot sign up today. A third-party article says non-partners can take it for $99. That is unverified, and Anthropic's own pages say otherwise.
    • Time: Anthropic publishes no prep-hours figure. It expects 6+ months of hands-on work with the Claude API, Agent SDK, Claude Code and MCP. The exam itself is 120 minutes: 60 questions, and you need 720 out of 1,000 to pass.
    • How to get it: through a partner-company login on the Partner Academy, pay, book a proctored exam with Pearson VUE (online or at a test center), pass, and renew every 12 months.
    • Name check: the audio said "Cloud Certified Architect", but that was a transcription error. The caption and the badge in the reel both say Claude Certified Architect. It is a real Anthropic credential, confirmed against Anthropic's exam guide. It is not an AWS, Azure or Google Cloud certificate.

  2. Generative AI with Large Language Models (DeepLearning.AI + AWS, on Coursera), S tier

    • Link: Coursera course page.
    • Cost: the certificate is paid. Its exact price only appears at Coursera checkout and could not be confirmed. Third-party roundups say $49-99 for a single course certificate, or $399/year for Coursera Plus (unverified). The course page does not confirm a free audit option or a free trial for this course.
    • Time: the page says "2 weeks at 10 hours a week", and its weekly breakdown adds up to about 17 hours. Self-paced.
    • How to get it: enrol, buy the certificate option, and pass 3 quizzes and 3 AWS labs. You need Python and basic machine learning first. Intermediate level.

  3. Google AI Essentials (Google, on Coursera), A tier

    • Link: Coursera page.
    • Cost: the page says "No, you cannot take this course for free." It costs $49/month in the US and Canada after a 7-day free trial. About 8 hours of content fits inside the trial, but the page does not say whether you keep a certificate earned during the trial after cancelling (unverified). There is no free version outside Coursera. Google's own page links to the same paid product.
    • Time: the page says 4 hours, but its five modules add up to about 8 hours. Self-paced, beginner level, no background needed.
    • How to get it: click "Enroll for Free" to start the trial, then finish all graded work in the 5 short courses. Cancel before day 7 if you do not want to be charged.

The tier board on screen matches the narration for all seven certificates, so these three are the reel's A and S tiers.

The full guide has each certificate's costs, steps and prerequisites.

items.title: Jev, TypeSafe AI's hosted decision model, and the 7 GitHub repos built on it
items.hook: Jev is real, but it is closed and paid per token; all seven repos exist, and they are free clients that still need a TypeSafe API key.
items.summary: A 9-slide carousel says Jev, a decision-making AI released on 15 September 2026, already has 7 open-source repos, and offers the full list to anyone who comments "Jev". The model is real: TypeSafe AI's hosted-only model returns a choice, a score or a yes/no with a confidence, and does not write text. All 7 repos are real and live. Five genuinely depend on Jev, one supports it as an optional provider, and one is a list. The post overstates things in places: it implies Jev is open (its weights have not been released), it names the wrong three capabilities, and it calls readers "early" after TechCrunch had already covered the launch.

Whether jev-ultrafast's linked site browser-use.com is actually affiliated with this repo (browser-use is also the name of a separate, pre-existing well-known browser-automation project) — the slide only shows the link as-is, ownership/affiliation is not otherwise established.
Full contents of the promised 'guide + repos' that the creator says he will send are not shown anywhere in the carousel itself.

followup.answer_html:
Jev is real. TypeSafe AI, a San Francisco startup, released it in early access on 15 September 2026, the date the post gives. Its CEO, Diogo Almeida, is a former OpenAI researcher. The launch is on the vendor's announcement, and TechCrunch covered it on 18 September.

What it is. Jev is a closed, hosted model that makes decisions. It does not write text. You give it unstructured text (or JSON) plus a typed question. It returns one of three outputs, each with a confidence:

  1. Choice: picks one option from a list you define.
  2. Score: rates something against ordered levels.
  3. Noul: yes or no.

Other specs from the model docs: current version jev-1.13.0, text input only, 64k tokens per request. TypeSafe's own blog calls it the wrong tool for chat, code generation or anything that needs a written explanation.

Where the post is wrong or overstates

  1. It makes Jev sound open. The repos are open source, but Jev is not. Its weights have not been released, so you cannot run it yourself. Every repo below is a client that calls TypeSafe's paid API.
  2. Slide 2 names the wrong three capabilities. It says "Choose / Score / Route". The vendor's three outputs are Choice, Score and Noul. "Route" is just something you do with a Choice result.
  3. Slide 2's sample output is made up. It shows a written reason field. Jev returns a decision and a confidence, not an explanation.
  4. "You're early, most people haven't heard of it" was already false when posted on 25 September. TechCrunch had covered Jev, demand had caused API outages, and the biggest repo had about 20k stars.
  5. The accuracy and speed claims are mostly the vendors' own. tax-doc-classifier's "100% accuracy across 261 IRS forms" comes only from its own README. TypeSafe's headline figures (up to 193.6x faster, 444.6x cheaper) come from its own benchmark, and TypeSafe admits they are probably at the high end of real results. Independent results are smaller and mixed:
    • TrueStandard tested 108 claims. Jev scored 96.3%, Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite 94.4% and Claude Haiku 4.5 93.5%. Jev was about 8x cheaper than Flash Lite and 27x cheaper than Haiku.
    • One developer quoted by TechCrunch found it 10 to 20x more expensive than Gemini on his workload.
    • KDnuggets points out that "zero hallucination" only means Jev cannot answer outside your list of options. It can still pick the wrong one.

What it costs

  • Self-hosted or local: not possible. There are no weights, so it cannot run in Ollama, llama.cpp, vLLM or Hugging Face. Some independent open projects copy the idea ("jeff", "OpenJev"), but they are not Jev and were not checked.
  • TypeSafe's hosted API (the only way to use Jev): $0.042 per million input tokens, and output is free. Limits are 1,200 requests per minute and 250,000 tokens per second, and TypeSafe can change them without notice.
  • Free tier: uncertain. Secondary reports say a $5 free credit (about 120 million input tokens) started on 21 September and was suspended soon after because of abuse. Whether it is back could not be confirmed. Check the billing page at console.typesafe.ai before counting on it.

The repos. The slides show exactly 7, matching the caption. All 7 are real, live GitHub repos. Four slides show no owner name, so those repos were matched by committer name and About text. All the code is free, but every repo except awesome-jev needs a paid TypeSafe API key to use Jev. Star counts below were checked on 28 September 2026.

  1. browser-use/jev-ultrafast
    • What it does: a browser agent from the browser-use team. Jev picks the next action and the page element; a separate text model is called only when text has to be typed.
    • Jev use: genuine, and central to the tool.
    • License: MIT.
    • Maintained: yes, but only since 16 September. Last commits 17-18 September, about 20.9k stars, new issues daily.
  2. tamaratran/fast-jev-compaction
    • What it does: a Claude Code plugin that replaces the built-in context summary. Jev decides which tool calls and results to keep or drop, and everything kept stays word for word.
    • Jev use: genuine, and required.
    • License: MIT.
    • Maintained: new, last commits 17 September, about 7k stars. There are 35 open issues with no visible replies from the maintainer.
  3. realZachi/pg-jev
    • What it does: a PostgreSQL extension. Functions such as jev(), jev_prob() and jev_choice() filter, rank and classify rows from plain-language conditions.
    • Jev use: genuine, and central. Your row data is sent to TypeSafe's API.
    • License: PostgreSQL License.
    • Maintained: new, last commits 17-18 September, 372 stars. Also listed on PGXN.
    • Other GitHub accounts host identical copies. realZachi's is the original.
  4. kyotofin/tax-doc-classifier
    • What it does: sorts tax document pages into 261 IRS form types before anyone works on them by hand.
    • Jev use: genuine, and central.
    • License: Apache-2.0 for the code. A separate DATA-LICENSE.md covers the IRS-derived data, and its terms were not confirmed.
    • Maintained: new, last commits 18-20 September, 471 stars. The one open issue says both install methods in the README currently fail.
  5. AkashPriyadarshii/jev-curate
    • What it does: a Rust command-line tool, with Python bindings, that cleans JSONL and Parquet training datasets by having Jev score each row.
    • Jev use: genuine, and built entirely around Jev. There is no local fallback.
    • License: MIT.
    • Maintained: yes. Last push 25 September, 87 stars.
  6. jev-chat/jev-chat-jarvis
    • What it does: an Android app that reads your chats (QQ, X, Feishu) and suggests two or three replies.
    • Jev use: optional. Jev is one of several interchangeable providers, alongside OpenRouter, DeepSeek and others, all using your own key. Calling it "built on Jev" overstates this.
    • The English phone demo on the slide does not appear in the repo, which shows a Chinese-language demo instead.
    • License: MIT.
    • Maintained: yes. Last push 28 September, about 6.8k stars.
  7. yibie/awesome-jev
    • What it does: a curated list of 100+ projects built on Jev.
    • Jev use: none. It is a directory and does not call Jev itself.
    • License: none.
    • Maintained: yes, frequent automated commits, last on 27 September, 1,865 stars.
    • Around 15 other "awesome-jev" lists exist under different owners. This one is the list the slide shows.

The comment gate. The post offers the "full guide + repos" to anyone who comments "Jev". The repo names are already on the slides, so the list itself is not hidden, and all 7 links are above. No public version of the "guide" could be found. The creator's site, gobiautomates.com, sells a $24/month membership called "AI Horizon", which is the name on every slide's footer. Neither the site nor the creator's GitHub mentions Jev.

items.hook: A ready-to-run checklist for the last mile before shipping a Claude-built site, each point paired with the actual tool and its real cost.
