followup.answer_html:
The checklist (reel's order, 20 points)

The reel's title card claims 20 things, and both the spoken audio and the on-screen list match each other point for point in the same order, all the way through. Wording below uses the on-screen phrasing (it matches the spoken line closely throughout, so nothing is missing or added). The reel's closing line, "and follow me for more," is not a checklist item and is left out.

  1. Privacy policy page
  2. Terms & conditions page
  3. Secrets off the frontend
  4. Force HTTPS
  5. Cookie consent banner
  6. Meta titles + descriptions
  7. Social preview image
  8. Add a favicon
  9. Sitemap + robots.txt
  10. Alt text on images
  11. Compress your images
  12. Check page load speed
  13. Fix color contrast
  14. Make it mobile friendly
  15. Custom 404 page
  16. Fix broken links
  17. Form validation
  18. Spam protection
  19. Set up analytics
  20. One clear call to action

How to actually do each point (Next.js/Vite/static, on Vercel/Netlify/Cloudflare Pages)

  1. Privacy policy page - Generate a draft with Termly or TermsFeed, then edit it to match what the site actually collects. Termly free plan: 1 policy, hosted only on their link, paid from $10/mo. TermsFeed: free hosted permanent link, premium clause add-ons roughly $13-$72 one-time. If the site collects nothing (no forms, analytics, or third-party scripts), a short plain-English page may be enough.
  2. Terms & conditions page - Same TermsFeed generator: free to use, free hosted permanent link, premium bundles from around $27 one-time. Often unnecessary if there are no accounts, payments, or user-submitted content.
  3. Secrets off the frontend - In Next.js only NEXT_PUBLIC_ vars ship to the browser; in Vite only VITE_ vars do. Check the built output or devtools for your key names. Catch secrets already committed with Gitleaks (free, open source) or turn on GitHub push protection (free on public repos, paid via GitHub Secret Protection on private ones). Any key already shipped to a browser must be rotated at the provider, not just deleted from the code.
  4. Force HTTPS - No tool needed. Vercel, Netlify, and Cloudflare Pages all auto-issue certificates and redirect HTTP to HTTPS by default, free.
  5. Cookie consent banner - Only actually needed if the site sets non-essential cookies (most analytics, ad pixels, embedded video/social widgets); strictly necessary cookies like session or security cookies are exempt under UK/EU rules. If needed: vanilla-cookieconsent, free and self-hosted, or CookieYes, free up to 5,000 pageviews/month, then $10-$55/mo by volume.
  6. Meta titles + descriptions - No separate tool. Next.js App Router has a built-in metadata API; just write a unique title (about 50-60 characters) and description (about 150-160 characters) per page. Free.
  7. Social preview image - Next.js auto-generates the OG tags from an opengraph-image file in a route folder. For dynamic cards, @vercel/og renders JSX to an image, free and open source. Preview how a link will look with OpenGraph.xyz, free.
  8. Add a favicon - RealFaviconGenerator, free, upload one image and get the full icon set plus markup (a dedicated Next.js version exists). Or in Next.js, just drop an icon.png in the app folder and it is served automatically, no generator needed.
  9. Sitemap + robots.txt - Next.js App Router: add a sitemap.ts and robots.ts file, no package needed, free. Otherwise, next-sitemap (free, open source) generates both as a postbuild step.
  10. Alt text on images - Writing the text is manual judgment. WAVE or the Lighthouse accessibility audit (built into Chrome DevTools, free) will flag any image you missed. Decorative images should get alt="", not be skipped entirely.
  11. Compress your images - Squoosh, free, open source, resizes and converts to WebP/AVIF entirely in the browser. Next.js's built-in Image component auto-optimizes on its own, no separate step.
  12. Check page load speed - PageSpeed Insights and Chrome DevTools' Lighthouse tab, both free, no install, give lab and real-user Core Web Vitals (good is LCP under 2.5s, INP under 200ms, CLS under 0.1). WebPageTest adds global test locations if you need more detail.
  13. Fix color contrast - WebAIM Contrast Checker, free: enter your two colors, it tells you if you pass WCAG AA or AAA. Lighthouse and WAVE also flag failing contrast across a whole page automatically.
  14. Make it mobile friendly - Chrome DevTools' device toolbar and Lighthouse's mobile checks, both free and built into the browser. Google's old standalone Mobile-Friendly Test is retired and now just redirects to the Lighthouse docs. Automated checks only catch the mechanical stuff (viewport tag, tap target size); also look at it on an actual phone.
  15. Custom 404 page - No tool. Next.js's not-found.tsx file convention handles it automatically, or drop a 404.html at the root on Netlify or Vercel for a static site.
  16. Fix broken links - Linkinator, free, open source, npm CLI, crawls the whole site including local files. Screaming Frog SEO Spider is free up to 500 URLs per scan, $279/year past that.
  17. Form validation - Client-side attributes (required, type="email") are UX polish only; they do nothing to stop a scripted request that skips the browser. Server-side validation is what actually protects the data - Zod (free, open source, 2kb) is the pattern Next.js's own docs recommend inside a Server Action.
  18. Spam protection - A hidden honeypot field (build it yourself in HTML/CSS plus a server-side check that rejects non-empty submissions) is free, invisible to real users, and needs no vendor account - the cheapest real option. For a managed widget: Cloudflare Turnstile, free up to 20 widgets/account with unlimited checks. hCaptcha's free tier has no stated cap; Pro starts at $99/mo for 100k evaluations.
  19. Set up analytics - Self-hosting Plausible or Umami is free forever if you run the server. Zero-maintenance free options: Umami Cloud's free tier (about 100k events/month, 3 sites) or Cloudflare Web Analytics (free, no stated cap, no cookies). Plausible Cloud starts at $9/mo once you want it hosted for you. Google Analytics is free with no pageview cap but trades away privacy-by-default.
  20. One clear call to action - No tool, a judgment call: pick the one action that matters most on the page, make it a visually distinct button above the fold, and de-emphasize competing links.

Where the reel oversimplifies or misleads

  • Cookie banner (point 5): presented as always required. It only applies if the site actually sets non-essential cookies, and which rules apply depends on where visitors are. A simple site with no analytics or embeds may need no banner at all.
  • Form validation (point 17): listed as one bullet with no distinction. Client-side validation is UX only and stops nothing on its own; only server-side validation protects the data. A site with just the browser's required attributes is not protected.
  • Secrets off the frontend (point 3): removing the reference from the code is not enough once a key has been served to a browser - it is permanently exposed through caches, git history, and CDN logs, and must be rotated at the source.
  • Privacy policy / terms & conditions (points 1-2): generator output is a template, not a finished legal document - it needs the site's real data practices filled in. The terms & conditions page may not be needed at all for a site with no accounts, payments, or user content.
  • Spam protection (point 18): implies a vendor service is needed. A free honeypot field needs no vendor account at all and is more private than a CAPTCHA-style widget.
  • Mobile friendly (point 14): Google's dedicated mobile-friendly checker is retired; there is no standalone tool anymore, only Lighthouse's mobile mode plus checking the site on an actual phone.
  • Analytics (point 19): "set up analytics" hides a real cost decision. Self-hosting is free with no limits, but cloud tiers have real ceilings a fast-growing site can hit.

Not in the reel (added here, not from the reel)

A live site also usually needs: error monitoring (for example Sentry's free tier) so a broken page gets caught before a visitor reports it; backups if the site has a database or user content; rate limiting on any public form or API endpoint so it cannot be hammered; and actually testing that auth-gated pages block a logged-out or unauthorized request server-side, not just hide the link to them in the UI.

followup.answer_html:
The four, resolved

1. godly.design - A curated daily gallery of well designed websites, apps, UI patterns, and page sections (hero sections, CTAs, footers, logos, app icons). No owner or company name is listed anywhere on the site. It is free with no login wall found on the homepage, the /websites browse page, or a third-party directory listing. No terms of service page exists (/terms returns 404), so there is no stated policy on screenshotting entries for reuse. What to do with it: open godly.design/websites, screenshot a page or section you like, and ask Claude to match its layout, spacing, and type, not the brand.

2. transitions.dev - A library of about 40 copy-paste CSS UI transitions (card hovers, modals, success checks, notification badges, tabs), run independently by Jakub Antalik. The free tier is real: no login requirement was stated, and the transitions ship as self-contained CSS with a license that allows unlimited personal and commercial use (you just can't repackage the library itself). Pro is $9/month, or $149 one-time for a lifetime solo license, and gates 36+ transitions total, React/TypeScript variants, a live-tuning tool called Refine, and a "commercial license" that mostly restates what the free terms already grant. What to do with it: install the free Claude Code skill (steps below) so the agent can apply a transition by name instead of you writing the CSS by hand.

3. animos.app - A browser tool that turns uploaded app screenshots into a short looping motion-graphics video (MP4/WebM), built by Herdetya Priambodo. The site itself only returns a JavaScript shell to a plain fetch, so none of the detail below is confirmed first-hand; it rests on Product Hunt, a review site (MakerStack), and search summaries, which mostly agree with each other. Most sources describe it as currently fully free, no watermark, no account needed for the core flow, but one summary says exports above 720p require a paid Pro plan, conflicting with the "fully free" reports. This is unresolved. The post's "25 templates" figure does not match any source; real counts range from about 30 to 50. What to do with it: drop a screenshot of your app into a template and export a loop, but check the export resolution and watermark status yourself before relying on the "no cap" claim.

4. deck.gallery - A curated archive of real pitch decks and brand guideline decks (OpenAI, Perplexity, Zapier, Discord, Nike, and others), run by a product designer named Muharrem. The "200+ decks, 9,000+ slides" figure is real, but it describes the $12/month Pro tier ($144/year), not the free tier. Free access is limited to today's new deck in full, plus 6 slides from each archived deck; email verification is required for Pro content. No download or export option was found on any fetched page, so treat it as browser-viewing only. What to do with it: browse today's free deck or the 6-slide previews and copy the structure (section order, slide count, information hierarchy) for your own pitch, not the exact numbers the post advertises.

Installing the transitions.dev Claude Code skill

transitions.dev's own instructions and Anthropic's current Claude Code docs describe different mechanisms that happen to land in the same place: a SKILL.md sitting in a folder Claude Code watches.

  1. Run npx skills add Jakubantalik/transitions.dev in your project (or anywhere, for a personal install). This is a third-party CLI, not an Anthropic tool. It writes the skill's SKILL.md into .claude/skills/ for a project or ~/.claude/skills/ for a personal install, which is exactly where Anthropic's docs say skills belong.
  2. Optional: run npx skills add Jakubantalik/transitions.dev -s transitions-polish for the "Polish" add-on that matches hardcoded animation durations to a token scale.
  3. Restart Claude Code, or if the skills folder did not exist before step 1, run /reload-skills to make Claude Code pick it up without a restart.
  4. Run /skills to confirm it loaded and see the exact slash name it registered under (transitions.dev does not publish this name in advance).
  5. Use it by asking Claude directly, for example "apply a success-check transition to this button," or invoke it explicitly with the slash command from step 4.
  6. Pro users only: run npx transitions-dev skill and complete the browser sign-in against an active subscription for the 36+ transition set, or npx transitions-dev add --pro to copy code directly instead of installing a skill.

Where the site and Anthropic's docs differ: transitions.dev only tells you to run the npx installer. Anthropic's docs additionally document the manual path (write the SKILL.md by hand in ~/.claude/skills/<name>/ or .claude/skills/<name>/, with YAML frontmatter) and a separate plugin system (/plugin marketplace add, then /plugin) that transitions.dev does not use. If you don't want to run a third-party npx package, you can build the same SKILL.md by hand, but the raw file content is not published on transitions.dev, only delivered through the installer.

Where the post overstates

  • animos.app's "25 templates": not supported by any source. Real counts run 30 to 50 depending on the source, and the true figure could not be confirmed directly from the site.
  • animos.app's free-tier limits: most sources say no watermark and no export cap right now, but one summary says HD and higher-resolution export needs a paid plan. Unconfirmed either way from the site itself.
  • deck.gallery's "200+ decks and 9,000+ slides": real numbers, but they describe the $12/month Pro tier. The free tier gives you today's deck plus 6-slide previews of the rest, not the full archive the post implies.
  • transitions.dev's "27+ transitions": this one holds. The skill page states 27+ for the free tier, matching the post.

No title correction is needed: all four have a working free tier you can use without paying, even where the headline numbers (deck.gallery's count, animos.app's template count) belong to a paid tier or a different source than the post used.

The comment gate

You do not need to comment "LINKS" for anything here. All four sites are named on screen in the carousel and in the caption, and the confirmed URLs are attached to this item below.

Left unconfirmed

  • godly.design: no owner, company, or curator found anywhere; no terms of service page exists to confirm a screenshotting policy.
  • animos.app: exact template count, the free/paid resolution split, exact clip length, whether a render queue exists for free users, and any paid-tier price (one reviewer's $10-20/month figure is a guess, not a stated price).
  • deck.gallery: whether an account is required just to see the free 6-slide previews versus only for Pro, and whether a hidden download option exists that a plain page fetch would miss.
  • transitions.dev: whether sign-in is required for the free tier, the raw SKILL.md contents, the exact slash-command name the skill registers under, and whether it appears in any official Claude Code plugin marketplace.

items.title: Connecting ChatGPT to your apps with Composio's MCP connector, as pitched in a delete-in-24-hours reel
items.hook: A reel says to switch on ChatGPT Developer mode, grab a link from connecttoeverything.com and name it "Composio" so ChatGPT finds recruiters and emails them. Composio is real, but that site is not Composio's.
items.summary: The reel tells viewers to turn on Developer mode in ChatGPT, make a free account on connecttoeverything.com, paste a link from it into ChatGPT as a connector named "Composio", and then have ChatGPT find recruiters and write outreach emails. It adds "I'm deleting this in 24 hours" urgency. Checks found that Composio is a real, funded company. connecttoeverything.com is not affiliated with it, returns no content and should not be used. Composio's official route is its ChatGPT plugin or its own link, connect.composio.dev/mcp. Composio is free up to 100,000 tool calls a month, but Developer mode needs ChatGPT Plus or above, on the web only. The toggle now sits under Settings > Security and login. Finding recruiters needs a paid people-search service such as Apollo or RocketReach, because Composio's LinkedIn tools cannot search people or send messages.

sections.heading: Image (media/4cad66124c14b023-01.webp)
sections.detail: This is not a frame from the actual reel — it is Instagram's own generic promotional/login-wall artwork (the kind shown when a video can't be fetched). It shows three overlapping phone-screen mockups with unrelated stock content: a pink/green abstract close-up of lips with a heart-reaction icon; a middle phone showing two people posing playfully (one with glasses making a peace-sign gesture near their mouth, one with braids and a necklace), with a reaction bubble above containing a crystal-ball emoji, eyes emoji, and exploding-head emoji, plus a like-button/progress-bar UI overlay; and a right phone showing a person holding a googly eye up to their eye with tongue out, with a green star-check badge and a profile picture (a person with green hair) in a colored ring. No legible text appears anywhere in the image beyond the emoji icons; no URLs are visible in it.

entities.name: ChatGPT
entities.why: The app the viewer is told to configure with Developer Mode/plugins to run the recruiter-finding workflow

entities.name: Developer Mode (ChatGPT plugins setting)
entities.why: Setting under ChatGPT > Settings > Plugins that the narrator says must be turned on first

entities.name: connecttoeverything.com
entities.why: Site the narrator says to visit, make a free account on, and copy a ChatGPT link from

note.spoken_transcript: I don't even know why I'm telling you guys this because you're all going to copy me and just get hired before I even apply. And I don't want that. So if you're seeing this, you're lucky. I'm deleting this in 24 hours. Go to ChatGPT, Settings, Plugins, and turn on Developer Mode. Now go to this exact website, connecttoeverything.com. Make a free account, scroll to ChatGPT, and copy this link. Come back to Plugins and ChatGPT, click Browse Plugins, hit this plus sign, paste the link here, and name it Composio. This is Composio. Now your ChatGPT can connect to all these apps at the exact same time. And just type this. It searches, finds the recruiters, and writes the emails for you. You are welcome. Go get a job, bro, and don't tell anyone I showed you.
open_questions: What is the exact link the narrator copies from connecttoeverything.com? Never shown/stated in words, only 'copy this link' pointed at on-screen — not captured in the transcript or the retrieved image.
What is the exact prompt text the narrator types to have ChatGPT search for recruiters and write emails? Only described as 'just type this,' never spoken aloud verbatim.
Is connecttoeverything.com a real, safe site, or is this an engagement-bait/scam funnel? Not something this read can determine — no research was performed per instructions.

followup.answer_html:
Verdict: Composio is real. The reel's website is not Composio's, and you should not use it.

  1. connecttoeverything.com is not an official Composio site. Composio's own site, docs, blog and GitHub never mention it. It returned no content on three tries, and search engines have indexed no pages from it. Composio's real addresses are all on composio.dev, and its real MCP link is https://connect.composio.dev/mcp. ChatGPT trusts whatever server sits behind a pasted link, whatever name you give it. Naming it "Composio" does not make it Composio. Whoever runs that server would get your Gmail once you approve it. If you already followed the reel, remove that connector in ChatGPT, remove any app you don't recognise at Google linked apps, and change any password you typed on that site. Do not confuse the reel's site with connect2everything.com, an unrelated Texas AV and cabling company.
  2. Composio itself is a real company. It raised $29M (its Series A post), its open-source repo has 30k+ stars, and it publishes its own security incident reports on its blog.
  3. The reel's ChatGPT steps are partly out of date. Developer mode exists, but the toggle is at Settings > Security and login, not under Plugins (OpenAI developer docs). You add connectors from the ChatGPT Plugins screen with the + button. "Browse Plugins" does not appear in any current source. Composio is also now listed in ChatGPT's plugin directory, so you can install it there without pasting any link.
  4. "It finds the recruiters" is overstated. Composio's LinkedIn tools can only post and read stats. They cannot search for people or send messages. Finding recruiters needs Apollo or RocketReach connected through Composio, each with its own API key. Gmail can then draft or send the emails.

What it costs

Side Plan Price Limit
Composio Free $0, no card, no time limit 100,000 tool calls a month. It stops at the limit and does not bill you.
Composio Scale $29/month Not needed for job hunting
ChatGPT Free $0 No Developer mode
ChatGPT Plus About $20/month (widely reported, not confirmed on OpenAI's pricing page) Cheapest plan with Developer mode. Web only.
Apollo / RocketReach API access Not confirmed. Apollo puts API access on its Custom plans. Only needed to find recruiters automatically
Gmail Free account $0 500 sends a day

So the reel's "free" means Composio is free. Developer mode needs a paid ChatGPT plan, and the recruiter search probably costs extra.

Setup, the official way (full steps, prompts and how to revoke access are in the attached guide):

  1. Make a free account at Composio's sign-in page.
  2. At chatgpt.com, go to Settings > Plugins, search "Composio" and install it. Then click Authenticate and Allow access.
  3. If that is not available, turn on Developer mode (Settings > Security and login). On the ChatGPT Plugins screen, click + and add Name Composio, Type Streamable HTTP, URL https://connect.composio.dev/mcp. Then Create, Authenticate and Allow access. Turn it on per chat from the + menu.
  4. In a chat, type @Composio connect my Gmail and sign in with Google.
  5. Use the guide's prompt. It lists recruiters, waits for you to confirm them, and saves the emails as Gmail drafts rather than sending them. Skip LinkedIn.

Key links: Composio's ChatGPT setup guide, Composio pricing, Composio docs, OpenAI Developer mode docs.

items.title: Anthropic's prompting playbook for Claude Opus 5.5 in the Claude apps and Claude Code
items.hook: Every tip from the 18 slides in one passage, checked against Anthropic's docs, with the post's three errors fixed and the Claude Code commands it leaves out added.
items.summary: Opus 5.5 always thinks before replying, works longer on its own and reports plainly. The passage covers all 18 slides: give the whole task with a finish line it can check, delete 'think carefully' lines and use effort (default medium) instead, write a CLAUDE.md rule naming the stops you want, split big audits across subagents, keep the task list in a file, and read what it needs from you first. It also covers the Claude apps tips, flagged messages, and fast mode. Anthropic's docs correct three claims: the safeguards line, the code review effort comparison, and 'keep permission prompts on' now that Claude Code starts in auto mode. It adds /goal, plan mode, hooks, the API breaking changes, and which general prompting techniques still hold.

sections.heading: Slide 1 — Title card
sections.detail: Photo of a man (glasses, curly brown hair, dark cardigan, white top) against a maroon background, with a dark circular badge reading "Opus 5.5". Text overlay: "Artificial Intelligence updater" / "ANTHROPIC PUBLISHED A COMPLETE PLAYBOOK ON HOW TO GET THE MOST OUT OF OPUS 5.5 IN CLAUDE AND CLAUDE CODE" / "Swipe for more". Decorative title card.

sections.heading: Slide 2 — Intro and "Try this first"
sections.detail:
Body text: "Opus 5.5 works well with the way you already use Claude. A few things behave differently, though: it works for longer on its own, it tells you plainly what it did, and it thinks before every reply. This guide covers how to work with Opus 5.5 in Claude apps and Claude Code, including how to prompt the model, steer a long run, and check your results."
Heading: "TRY THIS FIRST"
Subheading: "Three things to try in your first session with Opus 5.5"
1. "Hand over the whole task. Say what "done" looks like and when you want it to stop and ask. Then let it work."
2. "Delete "think carefully" lines. Opus 5.5 already thinks before every reply."
3. "When a long run ends, read what it needs from you first."

sections.heading: Slide 3 — Section 1: How to ask
sections.detail:
Heading: "1. HOW TO ASK"
Subheading: "Say what "done" looks like, then let it run"
"What to do. Give the whole task in one message. Name the finish line, like "the tests pass" or "every endpoint is migrated." Then let it cook."
"Why it matters on Opus 5.5. Opus 5.5 keeps going on long, multi-part work better than Opus 5 did. Compared to prior Opus models, its biggest gains are on multi-step work, like carrying a change through a large repository until the tests pass. Early testers had it run long coding tasks for hours with little oversight. With a clear finish line, it knows when it's done."
"How. In Claude Code, for example:"
Code block (label "CODE Text", button "Copy"):
"Migrate the payment endpoints from the old client to the new one.
Done means: every endpoint uses the new client, the old client is deleted, and the test suite passes.
Stop and ask me only if a test fails for a reason you can't explain."

sections.heading: Slide 4 — Figure A and "Stop telling it to think hard"
sections.detail:
Figure image titled "Say what "done" looks like, then let it run" with three labeled boxes:
"THE WHOLE TASK — Migrate the payment endpoints from the old client to the new one."
"THE FINISH LINE — Done means: every endpoint uses the new client, the old client is deleted, and the test suite passes."
"WHEN TO STOP — Stop and ask me only if a test fails for a reason you can't explain."
Caption line inside figure: "Give the whole task in one message. Name the finish line. Then leave it alone."
Figure caption: "FIG A — One message: the whole task, the finish line, and when to stop."

Subheading: "Stop telling it to "think hard""
"What to do. Remove "think carefully," "think step by step," and similar lines from your prompts and your saved instructions."
"Why it matters on Opus 5.5. Opus 5.5 always thinks before it replies, and it decides how much. You don't need to ask it to think. In our testing in a chat product, removing a "think carefully" line made replies start sooner, with no clear drop in quality."
"How. Delete the line. For a quick answer to a simple question, say so: "Answer directly." To change how much it thinks in Claude Code, change effort."

sections.heading: Slide 5 — Add to a running task; design guidance
sections.detail:
Subheading: "Add to a running task"
"What to do. If you remember something mid-run, you can type a follow-up while it works."
"Why it matters on Opus 5.5. Runs are longer now, so a restart costs more."
"How to do it. In Claude Code, type the message and press Enter while Claude works, for example, "Also keep the old endpoint names as aliases.""

Subheading: "For design work, name the styles you don't want"
"What to do. When you ask for a page, an app, or an artifact, list the design habits you want left out."
"Why it matters on Opus 5.5. With no design direction, Opus 5.5 falls back on a few default styles. A general instruction like "avoid a generic look" mostly swaps one default for another. A list of specific patterns works much better."
"How. Name the patterns:"
Code block (label "CODE Text", button "Copy"):
"Build a personal website with placeholder content.
Don't use a cream or off-white background, italic accent words in headings, numbered "01 / 02 / 03" section labels, monospace labels, [text cut off by horizontal scroll] pill-shaped buttons."
Body text: "Then look at what it chose instead. If you don't like that either, add it to the list and ask again."

sections.heading: Slide 6 — Section 2: Steering a long run (part 1)
sections.detail:
Heading: "2. STEERING A LONG RUN IN CLAUDE CODE"
Subheading: "Tell it which stops you want"
"What to do. Put a short rule in your CLAUDE.md file about when to stop and ask, and when to keep going."
"Why it matters on Opus 5.5. Opus 5.5 keeps you posted as it works. On a long task, it sometimes stops to report instead of going on: a summary that names the next step without taking it, an offer to continue, or a list of choices that don't block the work. It follows instructions that name these stops. Name the stops you want, too."
"How. Add this to CLAUDE.md, and edit it to fit your project:"
Code block (label "CODE Markdown", button "Copy"):
"When a step doesn't need my input, keep going. Put status notes in the same message as your next action.
Stop and ask only when you can't continue without me, or before anything destructive: deleting data, force-pushing, or changing anything outside this repository."

sections.heading: Slide 7 — Figure B and subagent intro
sections.detail:
Figure image titled "Tell it which stops you want" with a "CLAUDE.md" tag, two columns:
"KEEP GOING — When a step doesn't need my input, keep going. Put status notes in the same message as your next action."
"STOP AND ASK — Stop and ask only when you can't continue without me, or before anything destructive: deleting data, force-pushing, or changing anything outside this repository."
Caption line inside figure: "Edit it to fit your project. Keep permission prompts on for destructive commands too."
Figure caption: "FIG B — The CLAUDE.md rule: when to keep going, and when to stop and ask."

Body text: "If a run stops with "Want me to continue?" reply "continue." If that happens often, the rule above will help."
"A rule to keep going means fewer stops, so keep your own check before anything risky or hard to undo. The last line of the rule above does that. Keep permission prompts on for destructive commands too."
"For pair programming, you may want the opposite: a one-line plan before it starts and a short recap at the end. Say that in your CLAUDE.md instead. Opus 5.5 follows either one."

Subheading: "Ask it to split big work across subagents"
"What to do. For an audit, a migration, or a review across a large codebase, ask Opus 5.5 to split the work across subagents and check each result."

sections.heading: Slide 8 — Subagent prompt and Figure C
sections.detail:
"Why it matters on Opus 5.5. Early testers had Opus 5.5 coordinate parallel subagents on long audits and migrations, with little oversight."
"How."
Code block (label "CODE Text", button "Copy"):
"Audit every service in services/ for the retry bug in the linked issue.
Give each service to its own subagent. When a subagent reports back, check its evidence before you accept it.
Finish with one table: service, affected yes or no, and the evidence."

Figure image titled "ASK IT TO SPLIT BIG WORK ACROSS SUBAGENTS" / "Give each service to its own subagent" showing a box "Audit every service in services/ for the retry bug in the linked issue." branching into four boxes each labeled "Subagent", feeding into a box "CHECK ITS EVIDENCE — When a subagent reports back, check its evidence before you accept it.", then "Finish with one table." above a table header row: "SERVICE | AFFECTED YES OR NO | THE EVIDENCE".
Figure caption: "FIG C — Fan out to subagents, check each one's evidence, then finish with one table."

sections.heading: Slide 9 — Task list in a file; Section 3: Checking the result
sections.detail:
Subheading: "Keep the task list in a file"
"What to do. For a run that will take a while, ask Opus 5.5 to keep its task list in a file and update it as it goes. Then read the file, not the scrollback, to see where the run is."
"Why it matters on Opus 5.5. Runs are longer now. A long run fills the context window, and Claude Code then summarizes older turns. A list in a file survives that, and it shows you at a glance what's done and what's left."
"How. "Keep a checklist in TASKS.md. Tick each item when it's done, and add anything new you find.""

Heading: "3. CHECKING THE RESULT"
Subheading: "Read what it needs from you first"
"What to do. When a long run ends, look first for anything Claude is waiting on you for, like a decision it left open or a change it wants you to approve. Then read the rest of Claude's summary."
"Why it matters on Opus 5.5. Opus 5.5 reports on its work more clearly than Opus 5. Its updates and its final summary say what it did, what it found, and what it needs from you, in plain language."
"How. To change the summary's format, say so in CLAUDE.md, for example, "End every run with three headings: Blocked on me, Changed, Found.""

sections.heading: Slide 10 — Review the code / mark what it couldn't confirm
sections.detail:
Subheading: "Ask it to review the code"
"What to do. Ask Opus 5.5 to review a diff or a pull request before a person does."
"Why it matters on Opus 5.5. One early tester said Opus 5.5 at its lowest effort caught more bugs than Opus 5 at high effort, with fewer false alarms. It also explains its changes in plain language, so its pull request descriptions are easier to review."
"How. Feed this prompt to Claude:"
Code block (label "CODE Text", button "Copy"):
"Review the diff on this branch against main.
List only problems you'd block the merge for. For each one, give the file and line, why it's wrong, and how to show it fails."

Subheading: "Ask it to mark what it couldn't confirm"
"What to do. For research and analysis, ask it to say what it couldn't find or couldn't check."
"Why it matters on Opus 5.5. "I couldn't find this" is worth reading, and asking for it makes it easy to find."
"How. Add "Mark anything you couldn't confirm, and say where you looked" to the request. This works in a Claude research report and in Claude Code."

sections.heading: Slide 11 — Section 4: In Claude apps
sections.detail:
Heading: "4. IN CLAUDE APPS"
"First, check that the model picker says Opus 5.5."
Subheading: "Share the chart or screenshot itself"
"What to do. Attach the chart, diagram, screenshot, or slide. Don't retype the numbers."
"Why it matters on Opus 5.5. Opus 5.5 reads charts, diagrams, and screenshots more accurately than Opus 5, and it needs no extra steps to do it. It's also better at meaning that depends on where things are in the image: which boxes an arrow connects, what changed between two versions of a diagram, or when a meeting starts and ends in a calendar screenshot."
"How. Attach the image and ask a specific question: "Which of these services call the billing API directly?""

sections.heading: Slide 12 — Check a long document / ask for the finished file
sections.detail:
Subheading: "Ask it to check a long document"
"What to do. Give it a long plan, report, or deck, and ask it to find mistakes."
"Why it matters on Opus 5.5. Opus 5.5 pays more attention to detail than prior Opus models. In our testing, it caught a date that fell on the wrong weekday in a long planning thread, and a chart that didn't match the numbers in a deck."
"How. Submit the prompt: "Check this deck for anything that contradicts itself: numbers, dates and names. Quote each problem and say where it is.""

Subheading: "Ask for the finished file"
"What to do. When you want a spreadsheet or a document, ask for the file, not an outline."
"Why it matters on Opus 5.5. The spreadsheets and documents Opus 5.5 makes need less editing than Opus 5's before you share them."
"How. "Make this a spreadsheet I can share: one row per vendor, with columns for cost, contract end date and owner.""

sections.heading: Slide 13 — Settled answers in a project
sections.detail:
Subheading: "In a project, say when answers are settled"
"What to do. If follow-up questions in a long chat feel slow, add an instruction that earlier answers are settled."
"Why it matters on Opus 5.5. In a long chat, Opus 5.5 sometimes goes back over an earlier answer while it thinks about a short follow-up. That slows the reply."
"How. Add this to the project's instructions:"
Code block (label "CODE Text", button "Copy"):
"Once you have answered something, treat that answer as done. Focus on what I'm asking now, and don't go back over an earlier answer unless I ask about it or point out a problem with it."
Body text: "Leave it out of projects for long analysis, where a later step can show a mistake in an earlier one."

sections.heading: Slide 14 — Section 5: When a message is flagged (Claude apps)
sections.detail:
Heading: "5. WHEN A MESSAGE IS FLAGGED"
"Opus 5.5 is the first Opus model to launch with Fable-level bio and cyber safeguards. In Claude apps and Claude Code, most flagged messages move to an older model, and your work goes on there. Finding security vulnerabilities in source code is allowed, and everyday health and educational questions should still work. These safeguards can sometimes flag legitimate work, and we're tuning them to cut down on incorrect flags. If you're switched, here's what you'll see and what to do."
Subheading: "In Claude apps"
"What you see. A notice that starts with "Switched to" and the name of an older model. Claude answers on that model, and the chat stays on it."
"What to do."
- "To go back to Opus 5.5, choose it in the model picker. If the earlier message is still in the chat, it may be flagged again. Starting a new chat avoids that."
- "To be asked first, go to Settings, then Capabilities, and turn off "Switch models when a message is flagged." You'll see a "paused" card with your options."
"The check covers everything in the conversation, including files and search results. So a flag can come from earlier content, not only your last message."

sections.heading: Slide 15 — Flags in Claude Code; don't ask for hidden reasoning
sections.detail:
Subheading: "In Claude Code"
"What you see. A notice that names the older model. The session continues on that model."
"What to do."
- "Run /model to switch back."
- "Press Esc twice to edit your last message and try again."
- "To be asked first, run /config and change "Switch models when a message is flagged.""
- "Run /feedback if the flag was wrong."

Subheading: "Don't ask it to show its reasoning in the reply"
"What to do. Remove requests to reproduce its internal reasoning in the reply from your prompts and instructions."
"Why it matters on Opus 5.5. A request to reproduce its internal reasoning in the reply can be declined. It's one of the flag categories."
"How. Ask Claude for what you need instead, for example, "Explain why you chose this approach in three sentences.""

sections.heading: Slide 16 — Section 6: Speed / fast mode
sections.detail:
Heading: "6. SPEED"
Subheading: "Turn on fast mode when you're waiting on each reply"
"What to do. In Claude Code, use fast mode for back-and-forth work, where you read each reply before you send the next message."
"Why it matters on Opus 5.5. Fast mode is available for Opus 5.5 at launch as a research preview. You get the same model, and the text arrives sooner. It needs extra usage turned on, and it costs more per token than standard mode."
"How. Type /fast into Claude."

sections.heading: Slide 17 — Checklist (Figure D) and "Asking" section
sections.detail:
Heading: "YOUR OPUS 5.5 CHECKLIST"
"Run through this before your next long task."
Figure image titled "Checklist" with four labeled quadrants (each item has an empty checkbox):
"ASKING — The task says what "done" looks like / No "think hard" lines in prompts or saved instructions / Design requests list the styles to leave out / Charts and screenshots are attached, not retyped"

onscreen_text: ANTHROPIC PUBLISHED A COMPLETE PLAYBOOK ON HOW TO GET THE MOST OUT OF OPUS 5.5 IN CLAUDE AND CLAUDE CODE

Slide 2: Opus 5.5 works well with the way you already use Claude. A few things behave differently, though: it works for longer on its own, it tells you plainly what it did, and it thinks before every reply. This guide covers how to work with Opus 5.5 in Claude apps and Claude Code, including how to prompt the model, steer a long run, and check your results.
Three things to try in your first session with Opus 5.5
1. Hand over the whole task. Say what "done" looks like and when you want it to stop and ask. Then let it work.
2. Delete "think carefully" lines. Opus 5.5 already thinks before every reply.
3. When a long run ends, read what it needs from you first.
Say what "done" looks like, then let it run
What to do. Give the whole task in one message. Name the finish line, like "the tests pass" or "every endpoint is migrated." Then let it cook.

Why it matters on Opus 5.5. Opus 5.5 keeps going on long, multi-part work better than Opus 5 did. Compared to prior Opus models, its biggest gains are on multi-step work, like carrying a change through a large repository until the tests pass. Early testers had it run long coding tasks for hours with little oversight. With a clear finish line, it knows when it's done.
How. In Claude Code, for example:
Migrate the payment endpoints from the old client to the new one.
Done means: every endpoint uses the new client, the old client is deleted, and the test suite passes.
Stop and ask me only if a test fails for a reason you can't explain.
Slide 4: Say what "done" looks like, then let it run (figure)
Migrate the payment endpoints from the old client to the new one.
Done means: every endpoint uses the new client, the old client is deleted, and the test suite passes.
Stop and ask me only if a test fails for a reason you can't explain.
Give the whole task in one message. Name the finish line. Then leave it alone.
FIG A — One message: the whole task, the finish line, and when to stop.
What to do. Remove "think carefully," "think step by step," and similar lines from your prompts and your saved instructions.

Why it matters on Opus 5.5. Opus 5.5 always thinks before it replies, and it decides how much. You don't need to ask it to think. In our testing in a chat product, removing a "think carefully" line made replies start sooner, with no clear drop in quality.
How. Delete the line. For a quick answer to a simple question, say so: "Answer directly." To change how much it thinks in Claude Code, change effort.
Slide 5: Add to a running task
What to do. If you remember something mid-run, you can type a follow-up while it works.
Why it matters on Opus 5.5. Runs are longer now, so a restart costs more.
How to do it. In Claude Code, type the message and press Enter while Claude works, for example, "Also keep the old endpoint names as aliases."
For design work, name the styles you don't want
What to do. When you ask for a page, an app, or an artifact, list the design habits you want left out.

Why it matters on Opus 5.5. With no design direction, Opus 5.5 falls back on a few default styles. A general instruction like "avoid a generic look" mostly swaps one default for another. A list of specific patterns works much better.
Build a personal website with placeholder content.
Don't use a cream or off-white background, italic accent words in headings, numbered "01 / 02 / 03" section labels, monospace labels, [text continues off-screen] pill-shaped buttons.
Then look at what it chose instead. If you don't like that either, add it to the list and ask again.
Slide 6: 2. STEERING A LONG RUN IN CLAUDE CODE
Tell it which stops you want
What to do. Put a short rule in your CLAUDE.md file about when to stop and ask, and when to keep going.

Why it matters on Opus 5.5. Opus 5.5 keeps you posted as it works. On a long task, it sometimes stops to report instead of going on: a summary that names the next step without taking it, an offer to continue, or a list of choices that don't block the work. It follows instructions that name these stops. Name the stops you want, too.
How. Add this to CLAUDE.md, and edit it to fit your project:
When a step doesn't need my input, keep going. Put status notes in the same message as your next action.
Stop and ask only when you can't continue without me, or before anything destructive: deleting data, force-pushing, or changing anything outside this repository.
Slide 7: Tell it which stops you want (figure)
When a step doesn't need my input, keep going. Put status notes in the same message as your next action.
Stop and ask only when you can't continue without me, or before anything destructive: deleting data, force-pushing, or changing anything outside this repository.
Edit it to fit your project. Keep permission prompts on for destructive commands too.
FIG B — The CLAUDE.md rule: when to keep going, and when to stop and ask.
If a run stops with "Want me to continue?" reply "continue." If that happens often, the rule above will help.

A rule to keep going means fewer stops, so keep your own check before anything risky or hard to undo. The last line of the rule above does that. Keep permission prompts on for destructive commands too.
For pair programming, you may want the opposite: a one-line plan before it starts and a short recap at the end. Say that in your CLAUDE.md instead. Opus 5.5 follows either one.
Ask it to split big work across subagents
What to do. For an audit, a migration, or a review across a large codebase, ask Opus 5.5 to split the work across subagents and check each result.
Slide 8: Why it matters on Opus 5.5. Early testers had Opus 5.5 coordinate parallel subagents on long audits and migrations, with little oversight.
Audit every service in services/ for the retry bug in the linked issue.
Give each service to its own subagent. When a subagent reports back, check its evidence before you accept it.
Finish with one table: service, affected yes or no, and the evidence.
ASK IT TO SPLIT BIG WORK ACROSS SUBAGENTS
Give each service to its own subagent
Audit every service in services/ for the retry bug in the linked issue.
When a subagent reports back, check its evidence before you accept it.
FIG C — Fan out to subagents, check each one's evidence, then finish with one table.
Slide 9: Keep the task list in a file
What to do. For a run that will take a while, ask Opus 5.5 to keep its task list in a file and update it as it goes. Then read the file, not the scrollback, to see where the run is.

Why it matters on Opus 5.5. Runs are longer now. A long run fills the context window, and Claude Code then summarizes older turns. A list in a file survives that, and it shows you at a glance what's done and what's left.
How. "Keep a checklist in TASKS.md. Tick each item when it's done, and add anything new you find."
Read what it needs from you first
What to do. When a long run ends, look first for anything Claude is waiting on you for, like a decision it left open or a change it wants you to approve. Then read the rest of Claude's summary.
Why it matters on Opus 5.5. Opus 5.5 reports on its work more clearly than Opus 5. Its updates and its final summary say what it did, what it found, and what it needs from you, in plain language.
How. To change the summary's format, say so in CLAUDE.md, for example, "End every run with three headings: Blocked on me, Changed, Found."
Slide 10: Ask it to review the code
What to do. Ask Opus 5.5 to review a diff or a pull request before a person does.

Why it matters on Opus 5.5. One early tester said Opus 5.5 at its lowest effort caught more bugs than Opus 5 at high effort, with fewer false alarms. It also explains its changes in plain language, so its pull request descriptions are easier to review.
How. Feed this prompt to Claude:
Review the diff on this branch against main.
List only problems you'd block the merge for. For each one, give the file and line, why it's wrong, and how to show it fails.
Ask it to mark what it couldn't confirm
What to do. For research and analysis, ask it to say what it couldn't find or couldn't check.
Why it matters on Opus 5.5. "I couldn't find this" is worth reading, and asking for it makes it easy to find.
How. Add "Mark anything you couldn't confirm, and say where you looked" to the request. This works in a Claude research report and in Claude Code.
First, check that the model picker says Opus 5.5.
Share the chart or screenshot itself
What to do. Attach the chart, diagram, screenshot, or slide. Don't retype the numbers.

Why it matters on Opus 5.5. Opus 5.5 reads charts, diagrams, and screenshots more accurately than Opus 5, and it needs no extra steps to do it. It's also better at meaning that depends on where things are in the image: which boxes an arrow connects, what changed between two versions of a diagram, or when a meeting starts and ends in a calendar screenshot.
How. Attach the image and ask a specific question: "Which of these services call the billing API directly?"
Slide 12: Ask it to check a long document
What to do. Give it a long plan, report, or deck, and ask it to find mistakes.

Why it matters on Opus 5.5. Opus 5.5 pays more attention to detail than prior Opus models. In our testing, it caught a date that fell on the wrong weekday in a long planning thread, and a chart that didn't match the numbers in a deck.
How. Submit the prompt: "Check this deck for anything that contradicts itself: numbers, dates and names. Quote each problem and say where it is."
What to do. When you want a spreadsheet or a document, ask for the file, not an outline.
Why it matters on Opus 5.5. The spreadsheets and documents Opus 5.5 makes need less editing than Opus 5's before you share them.
How. "Make this a spreadsheet I can share: one row per vendor, with columns for cost, contract end date and owner."
Slide 13: In a project, say when answers are settled
What to do. If follow-up questions in a long chat feel slow, add an instruction that earlier answers are settled.
Why it matters on Opus 5.5. In a long chat, Opus 5.5 sometimes goes back over an earlier answer while it thinks about a short follow-up. That slows the reply.
How. Add this to the project's instructions:
Once you have answered something, treat that answer as done. Focus on what I'm asking now, and don't go back over an earlier answer unless I ask about it or point out a problem with it.
Leave it out of projects for long analysis, where a later step can show a mistake in an earlier one.
Slide 14: 5. WHEN A MESSAGE IS FLAGGED

Opus 5.5 is the first Opus model to launch with Fable-level bio and cyber safeguards. In Claude apps and Claude Code, most flagged messages move to an older model, and your work goes on there. Finding security vulnerabilities in source code is allowed, and everyday health and educational questions should still work. These safeguards can sometimes flag legitimate work, and we're tuning them to cut down on incorrect flags. If you're switched, here's what you'll see and what to do.
What you see. A notice that starts with "Switched to" and the name of an older model. Claude answers on that model, and the chat stays on it.
To go back to Opus 5.5, choose it in the model picker. If the earlier message is still in the chat, it may be flagged again. Starting a new chat avoids that.
To be asked first, go to Settings, then Capabilities, and turn off "Switch models when a message is flagged." You'll see a "paused" card with your options.
The check covers everything in the conversation, including files and search results. So a flag can come from earlier content, not only your last message.
What you see. A notice that names the older model. The session continues on that model.
Press Esc twice to edit your last message and try again.
To be asked first, run /config and change "Switch models when a message is flagged."
Run /feedback if the flag was wrong.
Don't ask it to show its reasoning in the reply
What to do. Remove requests to reproduce its internal reasoning in the reply from your prompts and instructions.
Why it matters on Opus 5.5. A request to reproduce its internal reasoning in the reply can be declined. It's one of the flag categories.
How. Ask Claude for what you need instead, for example, "Explain why you chose this approach in three sentences."
Turn on fast mode when you're waiting on each reply
What to do. In Claude Code, use fast mode for back-and-forth work, where you read each reply before you send the next message.

Why it matters on Opus 5.5. Fast mode is available for Opus 5.5 at launch as a research preview. You get the same model, and the text arrives sooner. It needs extra usage turned on, and it costs more per token than standard mode.
Run through this before your next long task.
