note.spoken_transcript: RAG versus OKF. Same goal, feeding AI your knowledge, but two very different ways. Here is the full map. Imagine a 50 page leave policy, and you ask the AI how many leaves you get in a year. Traditional RAG splits the PDF into small chunks. It turns each chunk into an embedding and stores it in a vector database. Your question comes in, the most similar chunks come back, and the LLM answers from them. But here's the catch. Page 2 says you get 20 leaves a year. Page 15 lists the exceptions. Similarity search can pull the right chunks and still miss how they connect. You get relevant pieces, not the full picture. That's the idea behind OKF, the Open Knowledge Format, an open spec Google Cloud introduced this year. Knowledge lives as markdown files, one file per concept, with a small YAML block on top for fields like type and title. Then the files link to each other with normal markdown links. Leave rules link to eligibility, and eligibility links to exceptions. So the knowledge becomes a connected graph, not a pile of random chunks. An agent can follow the links and get the full context. And because it's plain markdown, humans can read the same files the AI reads. Quick map. RAG finds similar pieces. OKF stores connected knowledge. They're not rivals, you can still search over OKF files. But when relationships matter, links beat guessing. Follow the account on screen, and comment the next topic you want explained.
open_questions: How does PageIndex compare to OKF and standard RAG?
How do you automatically convert existing corporate PDFs into OKF-compliant Markdown files?
What graph traversal strategies or tools do AI agents use when navigating OKF links?
How does PageIndex compare to OKF and graph RAG?
What specific parser implementations exist for OKF?

followup.answer_html:
Which approach fits which situation

  • One policy, or a set that fits in a ~1M-token context window: put the whole document in a cached prompt. For a 50-page policy on Claude Sonnet 5, that comes to about $0.008 per question once cached. This is an estimate that assumes about 25k tokens. The page-2 rule and the page-15 exception are both in view, so the problem the reel describes never comes up.
  • One or a few long, structured PDFs too big for the prompt: PageIndex. It searches a table-of-contents tree, cites pages and needs no vector database. Each query covers one document.
  • Many documents or high query volume: upgraded RAG. That means chunks split by section, contextual retrieval, hybrid keyword + vector search and a reranker. Add a one-hop expansion over cross-references extracted at ingest only if testing shows answers missing exceptions.
  • Knowledge you write and version yourself: store it as OKF, and retrieve from it with one of the options above.
  • Themes across a whole corpus: LightRAG. Use GraphRAG only if you accept that it is in maintenance mode and costly to index.
  • How to settle it: test the top three on 50 questions from your own documents. Make 15 of them rule-plus-exception questions where the two sit on different pages.

OKF: the reel's description holds up

Google Cloud's Data Cloud team announced OKF on June 12, 2026 (the reel's source post). In Google's words, it "represents knowledge as a directory of markdown files with YAML frontmatter" that agents can read "without translation".

The post sits under data analytics because the BigQuery team built it, and its worked example is a BigQuery table file. But it is framed around giving agents context, as the reel says. Version 0.2 (July 24, 2026) adds trust and provenance fields (v0.2 post). It is Apache-2.0 (repo, SPEC.md).

What the reel leaves out:

  1. It is a file format and retrieves nothing. Only type is required. Consumers must accept broken links, and nothing limits how many links an agent follows. In Google's own product, agents query through Knowledge Catalog APIs instead of walking the links (Knowledge Catalog post).
  2. Google ships no PDF-to-OKF converter. Its reference agent builds bundles from BigQuery. google-okf on PyPI is a third-party package despite the name.
  3. It is young: about 625 stars and no tagged releases.
  4. The name is shared. "OKF" also means the Open Knowledge Foundation, which is unrelated (disambiguation).

What else belongs in the comparison

  1. Long context + prompt caching: the baseline to beat for any corpus that fits.
  2. Contextual retrieval: the cheapest upgrade to plain RAG, done at ingest. Anthropic reports up to 67% fewer retrieval failures when combined with reranking (vendor figure).
  3. Hybrid search + reranking: catches clause numbers and defined terms that vector search misses.
  4. Agentic file search: the mechanism behind "the agent follows the links". It works up to roughly low thousands of text files.
  5. LightRAG: the maintained graph option, with incremental updates.
  6. Microsoft GraphRAG: the reference design for questions about a whole corpus. It is now in maintenance mode.
  7. ColPali: retrieval over page images, for scans, tables and charts.
  8. RAPTOR: the other tree approach besides PageIndex. It has had no commits since September 2024.
  9. Graphiti/Zep and Cognee: agent memory where facts change over time, not document retrieval.
  10. MCP: how to serve whichever option you choose to any agent.
  11. llms.txt: a site's starting-point file. It does not follow links.
  12. Evaluation tools: Ragas, DeepEval and TruLens. Without these, choosing between the options above is a guess.

Numbers that are claims, not independent results

  • PageIndex's 98.7% on FinanceBench was run by the vendor on its own system (Mafin 2.5 post).
  • The GraphRAG and LightRAG cost and latency figures come from an AWS benchmark (third-party).
  • The widely repeated $33,000 GraphRAG indexing cost is unconfirmed.

The PDF has the rest:

  • the full feature matrix across 11 approaches: status, how each works, updates, citations, cost and fit
  • install commands and quickstarts for each approach, taken from official pages
  • a recommended build
  • a 50-question benchmark plan with a rule for deciding between the results

extra_sections.heading: What OKF is, per its spec (verified)
extra_sections.detail: OKF v0.2 is a folder of Markdown files, one concept per file. Every file except the reserved index.md and log.md needs YAML frontmatter with a non-empty `type`. Recommended fields: `title`, `description`, `resource`, `tags`. Version 0.2 adds optional provenance fields (`sources`, `generated`, `verified`) and lifecycle fields (`status`, `stale_after`). index.md lists a folder's contents so an agent can read the bundle a level at a time, and log.md holds dated changes. Links are ordinary Markdown links, either from the bundle root (/tables/customers.md) or relative (./other.md). Consumers must not reject a bundle for broken links, missing optional fields or a missing index. Source: SPEC.md in GoogleCloudPlatform/open-knowledge-format.

extra_sections.heading: Current state, September 2026 (verified)
extra_sections.detail: v0.1 was announced June 12, 2026 and v0.2 on July 24, 2026. The Knowledge Catalog integration post followed on Aug 26, 2026. The repo is Apache-2.0, has about 625 stars and no tagged releases, and its last commit was Aug 21, 2026. Google's reference agent (Python, with a CLI) builds bundles from BigQuery (`enrich --source bq`) and renders them (`visualize`). It has no PDF import. Two PyPI packages, google-okf 0.1.3 and okflib 0.5.0, are third-party and untested. The google- prefix does not make the first one Google software. There is no independent standards body: Google controls the spec.

extra_sections.heading: How agents query OKF in Google's own product
extra_sections.detail: You publish a bundle with a one-time setup and `kcmd push`, an idempotent upsert meant to run in CI on every commit. At query time agents do not walk the files. They call Knowledge Catalog's searchEntries to find candidate concepts, then LookupContext for the concept body, then entries.get with view=ALL for the trust fields. Google publishes no cost or latency figures for ingest or queries. Outside Google Cloud, you supply your own entry-point search and link-following, capped at a small number of hops.

extra_sections.heading: Gotchas (confirmed)
extra_sections.detail: An entry point is still needed, because OKF is not self-indexing. Links drift as sources change, and the spec tolerates broken links silently. Nothing in the spec caps how deep an agent follows links, so over-traversal is left to the agent. Converting an existing PDF into concept files is work you do yourself or hand to an LLM. Searching "OKF" also returns the unrelated Open Knowledge Foundation.

items.title: Build Vision-Based PDF RAG Using ColPali and ColQwen2
items.hook: Learn how to build a Multimodal RAG pipeline that retrieves visual PDF pages instead of plain text chunks.
items.summary: Traditional RAG pipelines rely on OCR and text chunking, which destroy the layout and tabular structure of complex documents. By using ColPali/ColQwen2 vision retrieval, PDF pages are processed as visual images using patch-level multi-vector embeddings and MaxSim late-interaction scoring. The retrieved full-page images are then passed directly to multimodal LLMs like Gemini for accurate reasoning over tables, charts, and diagrams.

sections.heading: Slide 1: Cover
sections.detail: Introduction to building a RAG pipeline that reads PDFs visually like a human using ColPali vision retrieval rather than text-only parsing.

sections.heading: Slide 2: Overview & Tech Stack
sections.detail: Outlines stack components: colpali-engine 0.3.15, transformers 5.3.0 (specifically pinned), google-genai 1.75.0, torch 2.10, and model vidore/colqwen2-v1.0 (Apache 2.0). Runtime target: Google Colab T4 16GB or 8GB+ GPU.

sections.heading: Slide 3: Table of Contents & Why Normal RAG Fails (Target Slide)
sections.detail: Contains the complete 15-item roadmap index. Explains the core failure of traditional RAG: OCR extracts unformatted text lines (e.g., 'Q2 43.2 Q3 51.8'), losing column headers, multi-column alignments, and spatial context essential for business documents.

sections.heading: Slide 4: How ColPali Vision Retrieval Works
sections.detail: Explains visual retrieval via ColQwen2 (built on Qwen2-VL) and ColBERT-style late interaction. Generates visual patch embeddings and scores queries via MaxSim without needing OCR.

sections.heading: Slide 5: Architecture & Project Directory Setup
sections.detail: Diagrams offline index building (PDF -> images -> ColQwen2 -> .npy + metadata.json) and online querying (Query -> ColQwen2 -> MaxSim -> Gemini 2.5 Flash -> Answer). Defines project folder structure.

sections.heading: Slide 6: Dependency Installation & API Keys
sections.detail: Shows commands using `uv` to initialize project and install dependencies. Pointers for Gemini API key setup in `.env`.

sections.heading: Slide 7: Poppler & Platform Configuration
sections.detail: Details environment setup for Colab (`apt-get install poppler-utils`) and Windows (manual binary placement). Highlights dependency constraint: `transformers==5.3.0` due to `peft` compatibility.

sections.heading: Slide 8: Convert PDF Pages to Images
sections.detail: Implementation of `pdf_to_images` in `ingest.py` using `pdf2image` with automatic poppler path detection.

sections.heading: Slide 9: Poppler Helper, Resolution & Model Loader Init
sections.detail: Explains DPI choice (150 DPI for balance of GPU VRAM and sharpness) and RGB format enforcement. Begins `rag.py` implementation.

sections.heading: Slide 10: Model Loading Function (`rag.py`)
sections.detail: Defines `load_model()` using `vidore/colqwen2-v1.0`, configured with `bfloat16` on CUDA (or `float32` on CPU) and `.eval()` mode.

sections.heading: Slide 11: Batch Page Embedding (`ingest.py`)
sections.detail: Defines `embed_pages()` processing batches of PIL images with `torch.no_grad()`, offloading output tensors to CPU memory to avoid VRAM overflow.

sections.heading: Slide 12: Building & Saving Index
sections.detail: Defines `build_index()` saving individual page embeddings as `emb_{idx}.npy` and metadata to `metadata.json`.

sections.heading: Slide 13: Index Loading Implementation
sections.detail: Entry point for CLI ingestion and `load_index()` function in `rag.py` sorted numerically via custom sort key.

sections.heading: Slide 14: Query Retrieval Pipeline Setup
sections.detail: Completion of `load_index()` and initiation of `query.py` imports and query architecture.

sections.heading: Slide 15: Scoring and Top-K Page Retrieval
sections.detail: Defines `retrieve_pages()` using `processor.score_multi_vector` (MaxSim late interaction) to rank and return top-k document pages.

sections.heading: Slide 16: Call to Action
sections.detail: Prompting readers to comment 'RAG' to receive the complete guide and full script pipeline.

onscreen_text: Build a RAG That Reads PDFs Like a Human Colpali vision Retrieval
Your Next AI Project Shouldn't Be Another Chatbot.
Build a RAG that can actually understand complex PDFs.
Understands the document visually, like a human.
Finally... AI that actually understands PDFs!
Build a RAG That Reads PDFs Like a Human - ColPali Vision Retrieval
PDF with text, tables, charts, diagrams, layouts
Retrieve the right page by visual similarity
Runtime: Google Colab free tier (T4 16GB) or any GPU with 8GB+ VRAM
A RAG pipeline that retrieves the right page from a PDF by looking at it - not by reading extracted text. It understands tables, charts, diagrams, and complex layouts that normal RAG misses entirely.
You type a question. The system finds the most visually relevant page. Gemini reads that page and answers you.
1. Why Normal RAG Fails on Real Documents
1. Why Normal RAG Fails on Real Documents
Open any annual report, research paper, or legal contract. Now try to answer: "What was the revenue growth between Q2 and Q3?"
1. Run OCR to extract raw text from the page
3. Embed those chunks as plain text
4. Return a chunk that might say "Q2 43.2 Q3 51.8" with no surrounding context
The table structure is gone. The column headers are gone. The meaning is gone.

Complex document Tables, charts, diagrams, layouts -> Extract raw text Using OCR -> Chunk into pieces Split text -> Embed as plain text Create embeddings -> Return a chunk No surrounding context "Q2 43.2 Q3 51.8"

This is not a small problem - it's the default failure mode for almost all real business documents. Financial reports, legal filings, scientific papers, and medical records are all built around visual structure that OCR destroys.

The deeper issue is that OCR-based extraction was never designed to understand documents - it was designed to transcribe characters. Every table, chart, sidebar, and diagram it touches loses its spatial meaning in translation.
Rich visual structure (tables, charts, layouts) -> OCR -> Flattened text (loses meaning) "Q2 43.2 Q3 51.8" ...

ColPali (and its successor ColQwen2, which we use here) takes a completely different approach. Instead of extracting text, it looks at the entire page as an image and produces embeddings that encode visual meaning.
There are two ideas fused together inside it.

The vision part: ColQwen2 is built on Qwen2-VL, a Vision Language Model. It sees images the way a human does - it understands that a number inside a table cell has a different meaning than the same number in a paragraph.

The retrieval part: ColQwen2 uses ColBERT-style late interaction. Rather than collapsing a document into one vector, it produces a separate embedding for every visual patch in the page. When you query, each of your query tokens is matched against every patch, and you take the maximum similarity per query token and sum them up. This is called MaxSim scoring.
The result: a query like "revenue growth Q2 to Q3" matches the image patches that contain those specific cells in a table - even if no OCR ever touched the page.
What it can handle that normal RAG cannot:
Multi-column tables where row alignment matters
Scanned documents with mixed text and figures
Complex layouts: sidebars, footnotes, callout boxes
PDF File -> pdf2image convert pages to PIL Images -> ColQwen2 Vision Model vidore/colqwen2-v1.0 -> Page Embeddings list of tensors per page -> Index .npy files + metadata.json
User Query plain text -> ColQwen2 Encoder same model -> Query Embedding tensor -> MaxSim Scoring late interaction -> Top-K Pages ranked by score -> Gemini 2.5 Flash free tier -> Answer
Offline (do once): PDF -> page images -> ColQwen2 embeds each page -> save index to disk.
Online (every query): query text -> ColQwen2 encodes it -> MaxSim against stored embeddings -> top page sent to Gemini -> answer.

If you're on Google Colab, run this instead (Colab uses pip):

On Windows, poppler is not available via pip or an installer. You need to download the prebuilt binary and put it in your project folder. Do this once:
3. Extract it - you'll get a folder called something like Release-25.07.0-0
4. Rename that folder to poppler and place it inside your project root

Create ingest.py. Start with the imports and the PDF conversion function.

# ingest.py
import json
import pathlib
import numpy as np
import torch
from pdf2image import convert_from_path
from PIL import Image
The PDF-to-image conversion is a single function call, but there are a few settings worth understanding:

def pdf_to_images(pdf_path: str, dpi: int = 150) -> list[Image.Image]:
 # On Windows, point to the extracted poppler bin folder.
 # On Linux/macOS, poppler_path stays None (uses system PATH).
 poppler_path = _get_poppler_path()

On Linux and macOS, poppler installs to system PATH and convert_from_path finds it automatically. On Windows there is no system-level installer - you download the binaries as a zip and put them in your project folder. The helper checks for that folder first, then falls back to None (which means "look in PATH"). This makes the same code work on all platforms without any changes.

ColQwen2 accepts images at their natural resolution - it won't resize or warp them. DPI 150 gives you sharp text and clear table lines without creating huge tensors. DPI 72 is too blurry for fine-grained visual retrieval. DPI 300 works but uses significantly more GPU memory.
ColQwen2's image processor expects RGB tensors. Some PDFs render as RGBA (transparency channel included). The fmt="RGB" argument handles this automatically.
This is the shared model loader used by both ingest.py and query.py. Create rag.py:

# rag.py
import torch
from colpali_engine.models import ColQwen2, ColQwen2Processor
The model loader is a single function. The key decisions are device placement and precision:

def load_model() -> tuple[ColQwen2, ColQwen2Processor]:
 model_name = "vidore/colqwen2-v1.0"

 device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
 dtype = torch.bfloat16 if device == "cuda" else torch.float32

 model = ColQwen2.from_pretrained(
 model_name,
 torch_dtype=dtype,
 device_map=device,
 ).eval()

 processor = ColQwen2Processor.from_pretrained(model_name)

 print(f"Model loaded on {device} ({dtype})")
 return model, processor

Why bfloat16 on GPU? The model was trained in bfloat16. Running it in float32 on GPU wastes VRAM and gives no benefit. On CPU we use float32 because most CPUs don't support bfloat16 operations natively.
Why .eval() ? This disables dropout layers. Without it, you'd get slightly different embeddings every time you run the same input - that makes retrieval non-deterministic.
First run will download the model (~5GB). This is cached in ~/.cache/huggingface/ for all future runs.
Back in ingest.py, add the indexing function below your imports:
First, the function that embeds a batch of page images:

def embed_pages(
 pages: list[Image.Image],
 model: ColQwen2,
 processor: ColQwen2Processor,
 batch_size: int = 2,
) -> list[torch.Tensor]:
 all_embeddings = []

 for i in range(0, len(pages), batch_size):
 batch = pages[i : i + batch_size]

 inputs = processor.process_images(batch).to(model.device)

 with torch.no_grad():
 embeddings = model(**inputs)

 # Move to CPU and detach before storing
 # Each embedding is shape (n_patches, embed_dim)
 for emb in embeddings:
 all_embeddings.append(emb.cpu().detach())

 print(f"Embedded pages {i+1} to {min(i+batch_size, len(pages))}")
 return all_embeddings
Why batch_size=2 ? ColQwen2 uses dynamic resolution - each page can produce a different number of patches. Batch size 2 is safe for a T4 (16GB). Use batch_size=1 if you get OOM errors.
Why .cpu().detach() ? We store embeddings in RAM, not on the GPU. A 50-page document at 196 patches × 128 dims × float32 is ~5MB - easily held in CPU memory. The GPU is freed for the next batch.

def build_index(pdf_path: str, index_dir: str = "index") -> None:
 index_path = pathlib.Path(index_dir)
 index_path.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

 print(f"Converting {pdf_path} to images...")
 pages = pdf_to_images(pdf_path)
 print(f"Found {len(pages)} pages")

 print("Loading model...")
 model, processor = load_model()

 print("Embedding pages...")
 embeddings = embed_pages(pages, model, processor)

 # Save each page embedding as a separate .npy file
 pdf_name = pathlib.Path(pdf_path).name
 for idx, emb in enumerate(embeddings):
 np.save(index_path / f"emb_{idx}.npy", emb.numpy())

 # Save metadata: maps embedding index to source page info
 metadata = [
 {"index": idx, "pdf": pdf_name, "page_number": idx + 1}
 for idx in range(len(embeddings))
 ]

 with open(index_path / "metadata.json", "w") as f:
 json.dump(metadata, f, indent=2)

Why separate .npy files instead of one stacked array? ColQwen2 produces different numbers of patches per page (dynamic resolution). You cannot stack tensors of different shapes into one array. Individual .npy files handle this cleanly.
The index is just files on disk – you build it once and load it every time you query.

# rag.py (continued)
import json
import pathlib
import numpy as np

# Load all embeddings in order
 npy_files = sorted(index_path.glob("emb_*.npy"), key=lambda p: int(p.stem.split("_")[1]))

 with open(index_path / "metadata.json") as f:
 metadata = json.load(f)

 print(f"Loaded index: {len(embeddings)} pages")
 return embeddings, metadata
The sort key int(p.stem.split("_")[1]) ensures emb_10.npy comes after emb_9.npy, not before emb_2.npy (which is what lexicographic sort would do).

# rag.py
import torch
from colpali_engine.models import ColQwen2, ColQwen2Processor

def load_model() -> tuple[ColQwen2, ColQwen2Processor]:
    model_name = "vidore/colqwen2-v1.0"
    device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
    dtype = torch.bfloat16 if device == "cuda" else torch.float32
    model = ColQwen2.from_pretrained(
        model_name,
        torch_dtype=dtype,
        device_map=device,
    ).eval()
    processor = ColQwen2Processor.from_pretrained(model_name)
    print(f"Model loaded on {device} ({dtype})")
    return model, processor

def embed_pages(
    pages: list[Image.Image],
    model: ColQwen2,
    processor: ColQwen2Processor,
    batch_size: int = 2,
) -> list[torch.Tensor]:
    all_embeddings = []
    for i in range(0, len(pages), batch_size):
        batch = pages[i : i + batch_size]
        inputs = processor.process_images(batch).to(model.device)
        with torch.no_grad():
            embeddings = model(**inputs)
        for emb in embeddings:
            all_embeddings.append(emb.cpu().detach())
        print(f"Embedded pages {i+1} to {min(i+batch_size, len(pages))}")
    return all_embeddings

def build_index(pdf_path: str, index_dir: str = "index") -> None:
    index_path = pathlib.Path(index_dir)
    index_path.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    print(f"Converting {pdf_path} to images...")
    pages = pdf_to_images(pdf_path)
    print(f"Found {len(pages)} pages")
    print("Loading model...")
    model, processor = load_model()
    print("Embedding pages...")
    embeddings = embed_pages(pages, model, processor)
    pdf_name = pathlib.Path(pdf_path).name
    for idx, emb in enumerate(embeddings):
        np.save(index_path / f"emb_{idx}.npy", emb.numpy())
    metadata = [
        {"index": idx, "pdf": pdf_name, "page_number": idx + 1}
        for idx in range(len(embeddings))
    ]
    with open(index_path / "metadata.json", "w") as f:
        json.dump(metadata, f, indent=2)
    print(f"Index saved: {len(embeddings)} pages in '{index_dir}/'")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    import sys
    if len(sys.argv) < 2:
        print("Usage: python ingest.py path/to/document.pdf")
        sys.exit(1)
    build_index(pdf_path=sys.argv[1])

def load_index(index_dir: str = "index") -> tuple[list[torch.Tensor], list[dict]]:
    index_path = pathlib.Path(index_dir)
    if not index_path.exists():
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"Index directory '{index_dir}' not found. Run ingest.py first.")
    npy_files = sorted(index_path.glob("emb_*.npy"), key=lambda p: int(p.stem.split("_")[1]))
    if not npy_files:
        raise FileNotFoundError("No embeddings found. Run ingest.py first.")
    embeddings = [torch.from_numpy(np.load(f)) for f in npy_files]
    with open(index_path / "metadata.json") as f:
        metadata = json.load(f)
    print(f"Loaded index: {len(embeddings)} pages")
    return embeddings, metadata

def retrieve_pages(
    query: str,
    model: ColQwen2,
    processor: ColQwen2Processor,
    embeddings: list[torch.Tensor],
    metadata: list[dict],
    top_k: int = 3,
) -> list[dict]:
    inputs = processor.process_queries([query]).to(model.device)
    with torch.no_grad():
        query_emb = model(**inputs)
    scores = processor.score_multi_vector(query_emb, embeddings)
    scores = scores[0].tolist()
    ranked = sorted(
        enumerate(scores),
        key=lambda x: x[1],
        reverse=True
    )
    results = []
    for idx, score in ranked[:top_k]:
        results.append({
            **metadata[idx],
            "score": score
        })
    return results

followup.answer_html:
This is a build guide for a page-image PDF search tool: each PDF page becomes an image, gets embedded by the ColQwen2 vision model, and is matched to a question by comparing embeddings directly, with no OCR step. The top matching pages are then sent to Gemini as images, and it answers with a page citation, so tables, charts and layout survive instead of getting flattened into text.

The verified pinned set (checked 2026-09-28) is colpali-engine==0.3.18, transformers==5.17.0, torch==2.13.0/torchvision==0.28.0, google-genai==2.25.0. The model, vidore/colqwen2-v1.0, is Apache 2.0 and not gated, no Hugging Face token needed, but the real download is about 8.9 GB, not the carousel's claimed ~5 GB, because it also pulls an ~8.8 GB base model. No source states a minimum VRAM; a 16 GB Colab T4 is the safe target, and the carousel's "8GB+" figure is unconfirmed.

Gemini's answering step (gemini-3.8-flash) is free on the AI Studio free tier for both input and output. Google no longer publishes fixed RPM/RPD/TPM numbers, only a live per-account dashboard behind login, so check your own limits there before a bulk run. For one PDF under 1,000 pages / 50 MB, sending the whole file straight to Gemini is simpler and about as cheap as this pipeline; build the index only past that size, across many PDFs, or for scanned, handwritten or chart-heavy pages.

The carousel contradicts itself on transformers (5.7.0 on one slide, a hard pin to 5.3.0 on another), and the pin is stale: 5.3.0 was colpali-engine's old minimum, not a ceiling, and the ImportError it blames on that pin traces to an unrelated, already-closed transformers issue. The carousel also stops right before the Gemini call and holds the rest of the build behind a "comment RAG" gate. The item's comment_gate flag saying "not gated" understates that: the missing half, the actual Gemini call, the full scripts and the error handling, is exactly what got withheld, and the project document below writes that missing half from the libraries' own documentation.

extra_sections.heading: Verified stack, versions and install
extra_sections.detail:
colpali-engine: pin 0.3.18 (2026-08-22), not the carousel's 0.3.15; 0.3.18 fixed ColQwen2 LoRA weights being silently dropped under transformers v5. Its own maintainers now call colpali-engine deprecated, recommending Sentence Transformers v6+ (MultiVectorEncoder) for new projects; that path is covered as an extension in the project document rather than the main build, since it hasn't shipped long enough to be the safe default.

transformers: pin 5.17.0 (current), not the carousel's numbers. Slide 2 says 5.7.0, slide 7 pins ==5.3.0 and blames an ImportError (`_maybe_shard_state_dict_for_tp`) on anything newer. 5.3.0 is colpali-engine's declared minimum, not a ceiling: 0.3.18 accepts any transformers in [5.3.0, 6.0.0). The ImportError is a real string but traces to an unrelated, already-fixed dev-build issue (huggingface/transformers #45405), not a colpali-engine or ColQwen2 problem.

torch: pin 2.13.0 + torchvision 0.28.0, with cu126 wheels confirmed. Current stable torch is 2.14.0, but colpali-engine 0.3.18 requires torch<2.14.0, so installing the newest torch breaks it.

google-genai: pin 2.25.0. The old google-generativeai package is deprecated (support ended November 30, 2025).

poppler: Windows Release-26.09.0-0.zip (the carousel's example filename is about a year stale but the steps are unchanged); Homebrew 26.09.0; apt poppler-utils. Full per-platform install commands (Colab, Windows, Linux/macOS) are in the project document.

extra_sections.heading: The Gemini answering step the carousel never showed
extra_sections.detail: The carousel's architecture diagram names Gemini 2.5 Flash, but access to the 2.5 line is now limited to accounts that already used it; new projects should use gemini-3.8-flash, or gemini-3.5-flash-lite for a cheaper option. The current SDK is google-genai (the older google-generativeai is deprecated). The call pattern is: create a client with `genai.Client()`, then `client.models.generate_content(model="gemini-3.8-flash", contents=[...images and text...], config=types.GenerateContentConfig(system_instruction=...))`, reading the answer from `response.text`. PIL images can go straight into `contents`; the API allows up to 3,600 images per request, far more than any retrieval top-k. The carousel's own code stops at the retrieval function on slide 15 and gates this entire step, plus the full script and error handling, behind a request to comment "RAG".

extra_sections.heading: Free-tier limits and cost
extra_sections.detail: gemini-3.8-flash input and output are both free of charge on the AI Studio free tier. Google no longer publishes static RPM/RPD/TPM numbers in its docs; the rate-limits page only points to a live, per-account AI Studio dashboard that requires login, so real limits have to be checked there directly. If the free tier is exceeded, paid rates through 2026-12-31 are $0.75/1M input tokens and $3.75/1M output tokens (roughly doubling from 2027-01-01). Each retrieved page image costs about 258 tokens per 768x768 tile, so a typical scanned page runs to roughly 1,500-1,600 tokens; sending 3 retrieved pages plus a question is about 4,500-5,000 tokens, or roughly $0.0035-0.005 at the paid rate. For comparison, Gemini accepts whole PDFs up to 1,000 pages / 50MB directly at a flat 258 tokens per page, which for one modest PDF is usually cheaper and simpler than building this pipeline at all.

extra_sections.heading: Scaling past one .npy file per page
extra_sections.detail: Each page at ColQwen2's 768-patch cap is 384 KiB in float32 or 192 KiB in float16. 10,000 pages of embeddings alone comes to about 3.7 GiB (float32) or 1.8 GiB (float16), on top of the roughly 8.9 GB of model weights. Up to a few thousand pages, one file per page plus a full in-memory MaxSim scan is fine. Past roughly 10,000 pages, move to a vector store with native multi-vector MaxSim support: Qdrant and Vespa both publish first-party ColPali/ColQwen2 guides with real numbers (Qdrant's pooled-prefetch-then-rerank design is about 13x faster at ~99% of full-search quality; Vespa's binary-quantized MaxSim is 32x smaller in storage, with nDCG@5 dropping from 52.4 to 49.5 and recovering to 51.6 with a rerank stage). Milvus supports this only through a custom client-side retriever; LanceDB and Weaviate (v1.29+) support it natively but have thinner first-party ColPali documentation. colpali-engine's own hierarchical token pooling at factor 3 cuts vector count by two-thirds while keeping 97.8% of original performance, its own published number; no vendor publishes int8 (as opposed to binary) quantization numbers for these models.

extra_sections.heading: Newer checkpoints and the layout-aware-parser alternative
extra_sections.detail:
colpali-engine's own maintainers now call it deprecated in favor of Sentence Transformers v6+ (MultiVectorEncoder). Fully open, Apache 2.0 successors already outscore colqwen2-v1.0 on the legacy ViDoRe average: TomoroAI/tomoro-colqwen3-embed-4b (90.6) and athrael-soju/colqwen3.5-4.5B-v3 (90.9, though that one is an individual maintainer's checkpoint, not a lab). vidore/colqwen2.5-v0.2 scores similarly (89.4) but its backbone carries a non-commercial Qwen Research Licence. NVIDIA's Nemotron ColEmbed VL 8B v2 leads the newer ViDoRe V3 benchmark but is CC-BY-NC-4.0, non-commercial.

On the alternative path: for clean, born-digital PDFs, a layout-aware text parser undercuts the carousel's claim that OCR always destroys tables. Docling (MIT, local, free, self-reported table-structure TEDS 0.97) and marker (Apache 2.0 code, free weights under $5M revenue/funding) both preserve table and reading-order structure without flattening the page to one text stream. Page-image retrieval still earns its cost for scanned pages, handwriting, non-standard fonts, or charts where the visual layout itself carries the meaning.

extra_sections.heading: Evaluation
extra_sections.detail: The practical approach: hand-build 30-50 questions with known correct pages across a few real PDFs, covering a table page, a chart page, a multi-column page and a scanned page if one exists, then measure Recall@3 (the pipeline sends the top 3 pages), MRR and nDCG@5, and compare against simply sending the whole PDF to Gemini on the same questions. The formal tool for this space, illuin-tech's vidore-benchmark, evaluates a full custom pipeline through a BasePipeline subclass and pytrec_eval metrics, but its documented workflow only covers Hugging-Face-hosted ViDoRe datasets, not a private local PDF set; the project document's own eval.py fills that specific gap.

items.title: Security Checks for AI-Built Apps, Part 4 (Items 55-70)
items.hook: Part 4 excerpt, items 55-70 of a longer checklist. Sixteen checks, each with a test to run on your own app and the fix.
items.summary: Items 55-70 (Part 4) of a numbered security checklist for AI-built apps, shown in the reel as bare names. They cover authentication and business-logic flaws, CI/CD supply chain, fail-open checks and missing timeouts, LLM and agent risks, and browser storage, redirects and realtime endpoints. The earlier 54 items are not public.

sections.heading: Authentication & Logic Flaws (Items 55–59)
sections.detail:
55. No MFA: Missing multi-factor authentication on sensitive accounts.
56. Account Enumeration: User flows revealing whether accounts exist.
57. Business logic abuse: Flaws allowing unintended functional exploits.
58. Race conditions: Concurrency issues in critical operations.
59. Webhook replay: Missing replay protection on incoming webhooks.

sections.heading: Pipeline & Build Security (Items 60–62)
sections.detail:
60. Insecure CI/CD: Overly permissive pipeline settings or exposed credentials.
61. Untrusted build actions: Utilizing untrusted GitHub Actions in pipelines.
62. Unpinned build dependencies: Failure to pin and review action dependencies.

sections.heading: System Reliability & AI Safety (Items 63–67)
sections.detail:
63. Checks fail open: Security barriers passing by default on error.
64. Missing timeouts: Operations hanging indefinitely without timeout limits.
65. Sensitive info leak: AI features disclosing confidential data via prompts or outputs.
66. Invalid AI output: Executing AI output without validation or sandboxing.
67. Excessive AI permissions: Granting autonomous agents unrestricted access.

sections.heading: Client Storage & Endpoints (Items 68–70)
sections.detail:
68. Sensitive browser storage: Insecurely storing credentials/data in localStorage.
69. Open redirects: User-controlled redirection leading to phishing or exploits.
70. Unsecured endpoints: Insecure GraphQL, WebSocket, or real-time connections.

followup.answer_html:
Each of the sixteen checks now has an audit entry: what the gap looks like in AI-generated code, how to test for it in an app that already exists, and the fix, with the OWASP, GitHub, Stripe or vendor page behind it.

Three corrections to the post:

  1. Pinning an action to a tag like @v4 is not a safe middle ground. Per GitHub's docs, only a full commit SHA makes an action immutable.
  2. Items 65-67 map to the 2025 OWASP LLM Top 10 and the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications (December 2025). The post cites neither. Prompt injection triggers all three items, and the post never names it.
  3. Coding-agent permission defaults have changed. Current Claude Code starts in a classifier-reviewed "auto" mode, not one where a person approves every action.

The Hacker News citation now points at the actual comment shown in the reel. The OpenText citation could not be confirmed, so it has been removed.

This is Part 4 only. Items 1-54 are not published anywhere public. The caption's "resource doc" is sent by DM to people who comment, and there is no public link to it.

extra_sections.heading: What this is and why it matters
extra_sections.detail:
This reel is Part 4 of a numbered checklist. It shows items 55-70 only, as bare names, and every name is a standard security term used correctly. They share one pattern. AI code generators write the happy path: a login that works, a webhook handler that checks a signature, a workflow that deploys, an agent that can act. They leave out the defensive half: a second factor, uniform error messages, atomic updates, replay windows, pinned actions, deny-on-error, timeouts, scoped retrieval, output encoding, least-privilege tools, HttpOnly cookies, redirect allowlists and locked-down GraphQL.

The sections below turn each name into an audit entry. Each one covers what the gap looks like in generated code, how to test an existing app for it, and the fix, with the authoritative reference. Items 55-59 and 68-70 are classic web flaws. Items 60-62 are pipeline supply chain. Items 63-64 are design principles that apply in CI and at runtime. Items 65-67 are the LLM and agent checks, where the post's framing lags the current OWASP lists.

extra_sections.heading: Audit: Authentication & Logic Flaws (Items 55-59)
extra_sections.detail:
**55. No MFA.**
*Flaw:* Generated auth is email plus password. MFA touches enrollment, factor delivery, recovery codes and step-up, so it rarely gets built unless someone asks for it.
*Check:* Log in as owner, admin and billing roles and see whether a second factor is ever required. Then, from a logged-in session, change the email or password, disable MFA, create an API key or change payment details. Note whether anything asks you to verify again.
*Fix:* Require MFA on every account, and always on privileged roles. Use TOTP or stronger; OWASP rates SMS-only as the weakest acceptable option. Add step-up verification before password or email changes, before disabling MFA and before admin elevation. Prompt again on a new device or IP. See the [OWASP MFA Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Multifactor_Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.html).

**56. Account enumeration.**
*Flaw:* Generated login code often returns "user not found" early, before checking the password. The message, the status code or the response time then differs for real accounts. Signup forms often say "email already registered".
*Check:* On login (real user with a wrong password vs unknown user), signup and forgot-password, send both cases. Compare the response body, the status code and the timing. Any difference confirms enumeration.
*Fix:* Return one message and one status for a wrong password, an unknown user and a locked account. Password reset always says "if an account exists, we sent a link". Signup accepts every address and emails either way; an existing user gets a note that someone tried to register. For unknown users, compare against a dummy hash so the timing matches. See the [OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.html) and the [Forgot Password Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Forgot_Password_Cheat_Sheet.html).

**57. Business logic abuse.**
*Flaw:* Each endpoint is generated on its own. It checks that a field is a number, but not that it is non-negative, one-time-use or in sequence. Multi-step flows trust the client to say which step it is on.
*Check:* Call the API directly and skip the UI. Try:
- negative quantities
- the same coupon twice in one request
- checkout step 3 without steps 1 and 2
- a referral bonus on your own account
- a promo or signup-bonus endpoint hit back to back

*Fix:* Keep the flow state on the server as a state machine, and reject steps that arrive out of order or repeat. Give bonus, referral and promo endpoints their own rate limits, separate from general API limits. Write adversarial tests for each flow: skip a step, reorder, repeat, race. See the [OWASP Business Logic Security Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Business_Logic_Security_Cheat_Sheet.html).

**58. Race conditions.**
*Flaw:* Generated handlers read a row, compute in app code, then write the row back. Two concurrent requests read the same value, so a one-time coupon redeems twice, stock goes negative or a balance ends up wrong. The reel's diagram shows this exact lost update: two processes both read a balance of 100, and the final value is wrong.
*Check:* Send 10-50 identical requests in parallel to a check-then-act endpoint (redeem coupon, withdraw, decrement stock, claim a limited item). Compare the result with what the same requests would produce one after another.
*Fix:* Make the check and the write one atomic database operation. Options:
- a conditional update such as `UPDATE inventory SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE id = ? AND qty > 0`, then check how many rows it changed
- `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` inside a transaction at REPEATABLE READ or higher
- optimistic locking with a version column

Prefer these to app-level locks. For queued work, use idempotency keys so duplicate requests run once. See [OWASP: Race Conditions](https://community.owasp.org/pages/vulnerabilities/race_conditions).

**59. Webhook replay.**
*Flaw:* Generated handlers verify the HMAC signature and stop there. A captured valid payload stays valid forever, so sending it again fulfills the order again or applies the credit again.
*Check:* Take a real webhook that was already processed (headers and raw body), from your logs or the provider's resend feature, and POST it again later. If the side effect happens a second time, replay protection is missing. In the code, look for a timestamp tolerance check and a record of processed event IDs.
*Fix:*
- Verify with the provider's official library, over the raw body.
- Reject signed timestamps outside a small window. Stripe's libraries default to 5 minutes, and a tolerance of 0 turns the check off.
- Record processed event IDs and reject repeats. This also catches replays that arrive inside the window.

See [Stripe: Receive events in your webhook endpoint](https://docs.stripe.com/webhooks).

extra_sections.heading: Audit: Pipeline & Build Security (Items 60-62)
extra_sections.detail:
**60. Insecure CI/CD.**
*Flaw:* Scaffolded GitHub Actions workflows leave out a `permissions:` block and keep long-lived cloud keys as repository secrets. The pipeline can then write to the repo, publish and deploy, and one leaked secret reaches production. GitHub's current default is safer than the post implies. Repositories created since February 2023 get a read-only `GITHUB_TOKEN` for contents and packages. Older repos and orgs may still default to read and write. Today the risk is mostly a legacy default or a setting someone widened.
*Check:*
- Settings > Actions > General > Workflow permissions. "Read and write" is too broad.
- Grep every workflow for a `permissions:` key.
- Search workflows and secrets for `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, `AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET` and similar keys.

*Fix:* Set the default to read-only. Add explicit `permissions:` to each job (for example `contents: read`), and grant more only where a job needs it. Replace static cloud keys with OIDC, so jobs get short-lived tokens and GitHub stores no long-lived credential. See [Controlling permissions for GITHUB_TOKEN](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/writing-workflows/choosing-what-your-workflow-does/controlling-permissions-for-github_token) and [Security hardening with OpenID Connect](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/security-for-github-actions/security-hardening-your-deployments/about-security-hardening-with-openid-connect).

**61. Untrusted build actions.**
*Flaw:* Generated workflows pull in whatever third-party action a tutorial used. Every action runs with the job's environment and every secret exposed to that job.
*Check:* List every `uses:` line. For anything not from `actions/*` or a verified creator, confirm three things: it comes from the real upstream repo, not a fork; someone has read its source; and the job really needs the secrets the action can see.
*Fix:* Prefer actions from GitHub or verified creators. Read the source of anything else, and limit which secrets each job gets. At org level, Settings > Actions > General > "Allow select actions and reusable workflows" can block unapproved actions. Since August 2025 it can also require SHA pinning. See [Security hardening for GitHub Actions](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/security-for-github-actions/security-guides/security-hardening-for-github-actions) and the [GitHub changelog entry](https://github.blog/changelog/2025-08-15-github-actions-policy-now-supports-blocking-and-sha-pinning-actions/).

**62. Unpinned build dependencies.**
*Flaw:* `@v4` or `@main` runs whatever the tag points at on the day of the run. If the maintainer, or someone who compromised the repo, moves the tag, new code runs with the old trust. The post calls this "not pinned or reviewed", but tag pinning is not a safe halfway point: GitHub's docs say a full-length commit SHA is the only way to use an action as an immutable release.
*Check:* Grep workflows for `uses:` lines that do not end in a 40-character SHA. Check whether Dependabot or a similar bot is set up to propose updates.
*Fix:* Write `uses: owner/action@<40-char-sha> # v4`, with the SHA taken from the real upstream repo. Let Dependabot propose SHA bumps so pinned actions still get reviewed updates and do not go stale. For package dependencies, enforce lockfiles and verify versions by hash.

The reel's citation for this item is a [Hacker News comment in the 2018 event-stream npm backdoor thread](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=18534689): "If you aren't reviewing the diffs of your dependencies when you update them, you're trusting random strangers on the Internet to run code on your systems." The [OWASP CI/CD Security Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/CI_CD_Security_Cheat_Sheet.html) covers least privilege, pinning and deny-by-default for the whole pipeline.

extra_sections.heading: Audit: System Reliability & AI Safety (Items 63-67)
extra_sections.detail:
**63. Checks fail open.** This applies both in CI and at runtime.
*Flaw:* Generated code wraps an auth check, permission check or rate limiter in try/catch and returns "allowed" when it errors. In CI, a scanner step errors and the pipeline carries on. Either way, the check gives way exactly when something has already gone wrong.
*Check (code):* Read every catch/except in auth, permission and rate-limit functions. Anything that returns true or "allowed" fails open. Also test what the app does when its auth service or cache is down.
*Check (CI):* Look for security steps marked `continue-on-error: true` or whose exit code is ignored. Check whether they are required status checks in branch protection.
*Fix:* Every error path returns deny, the same path a refused operation takes. Remove `continue-on-error` from security gates and make them required checks. No single setting fixes this; every place the app makes a security decision needs checking. See [OWASP: Fail Securely](https://community.owasp.org/Fail_securely). The reel's citation card for this item names an OpenText Community article, "Security Fundamentals Part 1: Fail Open vs. Fail Closed". A page with that title turned up in search but could not be read, so it is not linked here.

**64. Missing timeouts.**
*Flaw:* Generated HTTP, database and RPC clients use library defaults, and those are often no timeout at all (Python `requests`, axios). One slow dependency then holds request threads until the app stops responding. In CI, GitHub-hosted runners cap a job at 360 minutes by default. That is far too long to catch a hang, and self-hosted runners can run longer.
*Check:*
- `requests` calls without `timeout=`
- fetch or axios calls without a timeout or `AbortController` signal
- database pools and gRPC clients without connect or read timeouts
- workflows without `timeout-minutes:` on jobs and long steps

*Fix:* Set explicit connect and read timeouts on every outbound call, with bounded retry and backoff. Set `timeout-minutes` on every job and every long step.

**One trigger behind items 65-67: prompt injection** ([LLM01:2025](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm01-prompt-injection/)). An instruction hidden in a web page, document or email the model reads can leak data (65), produce the payload your code executes (66) and steer an agent's tools (67), all at once. OWASP says it is unclear whether fool-proof prevention exists. The defense is layers: the controls below, human approval for high-risk actions, and adversarial testing.

**65. Sensitive info leak.** Maps to [LLM02:2025 Sensitive Information Disclosure](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm022025-sensitive-information-disclosure/) and [LLM07:2025 System Prompt Leakage](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm072025-system-prompt-leakage/).
*Flaw:* Common leaks in generated code:
- secrets, internal URLs or business rules in the system prompt
- a shared vector index queried with no user or tenant filter
- memory or response caches shared across tenants
- raw prompts and completions sent to logging, analytics or third-party APIs

*Check:*
- Read the system prompt for anything you would not publish, then ask the model to repeat its instructions.
- As user A, search for content only user B has.
- List everywhere prompts and completions are logged, and how long each provider keeps them.
- Look for database rows or environment values pasted into prompts.

*Fix:* Keep secrets and enforcement rules out of the system prompt, and enforce authorization in code, outside the model. Scope retrieval in the query itself (a `tenant_id` filter or a per-tenant namespace), not through prompt instructions. Redact before logging or display. Use zero-data-retention terms where offered, and check each tool: eligibility differs even within one vendor, and Anthropic marks its code execution tool as not eligible.

**66. Invalid AI output.** Maps to [LLM05:2025 Improper Output Handling](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm052025-improper-output-handling/).
*Flaw:* Model output flows somewhere that runs or renders it:
- `eval`, `exec` or a shell: remote code execution
- SQL built by string concatenation: injection
- the DOM as HTML or Markdown: XSS
- file paths: path traversal

*Check:* Grep for `eval(`, `exec(`, `new Function(`, `child_process.exec` and `os.system` fed by model output. Look for SQL built with f-strings or concatenation, and for `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, `v-html` or `.innerHTML =` fed by model text. Find any tool that runs a model-written command verbatim.
*Fix:* Treat the model as an untrusted user. Use parameterized queries, context-aware output encoding, an HTML sanitizer such as DOMPurify and a strict Content-Security-Policy. Give the model narrow typed tools instead of a free-text "run this" tool. When generated code must run, sandbox it. Anthropic's [code execution tool](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/code-execution-tool) runs in a container with no internet access. Its open-source sandbox-runtime wraps a process with OS-level isolation (bubblewrap on Linux, Seatbelt on macOS); see [sandbox environments](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandbox-environments).

**67. Excessive AI permissions.** Maps to [LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm062025-excessive-agency/). For autonomous agents it also maps to ASI02 Tool Misuse and ASI03 Identity & Privilege Abuse in the [OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications](https://genai.owasp.org/2025/12/09/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-the-benchmark-for-agentic-security-in-the-age-of-autonomous-ai/).
*Flaw:*
- a broad tool ("run any SQL", "write anywhere") where a narrow one would do
- long-lived shared credentials embedded in tool or MCP server definitions
- irreversible actions (delete, deploy, merge, send, spend) with no human approval

*Check:*
- List every tool and the real privilege of the credential behind it, and try to make a read tool write.
- Look for static keys in tool and MCP configs.
- Ask the agent to do something irreversible and see whether it stops for approval.
- Confirm which permission mode your coding agent actually starts in.

*Fix:*
- Scope each tool (read vs write, allowed paths and operations, blocked patterns) instead of giving open shell access.
- Use short-lived, per-user scoped tokens.
- Redact `password`, `api_key`, `token`, `secret` and `credential` parameters from logs.
- Require step-up approval for payments, privilege changes, bulk deletion and production deploys, bound to the exact parameters and expiring quickly.

See the [OWASP AI Agent Security Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/AI_Agent_Security_Cheat_Sheet.html).

**Where the post is out of step on 65-67**
1. The post gives no OWASP mapping, apart from an LLM02 label in one diagram. The current IDs come from the 2025 list. Improper Output Handling moved from LLM02 (2023) to LLM05, Excessive Agency moved from LLM08 to LLM06, and System Prompt Leakage (LLM07) is new. Checklists that cite older LLM0x numbers point at the wrong entries. The full current list is the [OWASP Top 10 for LLM/GenAI Applications](https://genai.owasp.org/llm-top-10/).
2. The post never mentions prompt injection, which triggers all three items.
3. Item 67 now has its own list, the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications (ASI01-ASI10), published December 2025. Its ASI01 Agent Goal Hijack is the injection-driven form of this item.
4. Agent permission defaults have changed. As of v2.1.283, Claude Code starts interactive sessions in "auto" mode on every plan. In auto mode a classifier model, not a person, reviews each action. By default it blocks production deploys, permission grants, force pushes, mass deletion and secret exfiltration. The [permission-mode docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes) say auto mode "does not guarantee safety" and that `bypassPermissions` belongs only inside containers, VMs or the sandbox runtime. Advice that assumes coding agents ask before every action is out of date for this tool.
5. The reel's item-67 dropdown ("Default permissions / Auto-review / Full access") matches no single product's current labels. Read it as an illustration. The item-66 diagram is research, not a feature (see the diagrams section).

extra_sections.heading: Audit: Client Storage & Endpoints (Items 68-70)
extra_sections.detail:
**68. Sensitive browser storage.**
*Flaw:* Generated auth stores the JWT or session token in `localStorage`, because it takes one line to set and read. Any script on the page's origin can read it, so a single XSS exposes every token. sessionStorage and IndexedDB have the same exposure.
*Check:* Open DevTools > Application (Chrome) or Storage (Firefox). Look in Local Storage, Session Storage and IndexedDB for JWTs, API keys, session IDs, or keys named like `token` or `supabase.auth.token`. Grep the frontend for `localStorage.setItem` near login code. Decode any token you find to see what it can do.
*Fix:* Use a cookie set by the server as `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax` (or Strict). The alternative is a backend-for-frontend that keeps tokens on the server and gives the browser only an opaque session cookie. HttpOnly is what stops XSS from reading the token. SameSite adds CSRF defense in depth but does not replace CSRF tokens. Keep web storage for non-sensitive UI state. See the [OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Session_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html) and the [HTML5 Security Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/HTML5_Security_Cheat_Sheet.html).

**69. Open redirects.**
*Flaw:* "Return to where you were" gets built as a 302 to a raw `next`, `redirect` or `returnUrl` parameter. A link that starts on your trusted domain and lands on an attacker's site works well for phishing and OAuth token theft. Forwards can also reach internal functions and skip access checks.
*Check:* Find every endpoint that takes `redirect`, `next`, `returnTo`, `url` or `callback` and returns a 3xx. Try `https://evil.example.com`, `//evil.example.com` and `/\evil.example.com`. If the Location header leaves your site, the redirect is open.
*Fix:* OWASP's first choice is to take no URL from the user at all: map a short ID to a destination stored on the server. Otherwise, allow only relative same-origin paths (reject anything with a scheme or a leading `//`) or an explicit host allowlist. Show a confirmation page before any allowed off-site redirect. See the [OWASP Unvalidated Redirects and Forwards Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Unvalidated_Redirects_and_Forwards_Cheat_Sheet.html).

**70. Unsecured endpoints.**
*GraphQL flaw:* Scaffolded servers keep development defaults in production: introspection and GraphiQL on, no depth or cost limit, verbose errors.
*Check:* Send `{ __schema { types { name } } }` to the production `/graphql` endpoint. Send a deeply nested query, then a batch of 50 or more aliased copies of an expensive query, and watch the latency. Look for stack traces in error responses.
*Fix:*
- Turn off introspection and GraphiQL in production.
- Add a depth limit (for example graphql-depth-limit) and a cost or complexity limit; depth alone misses wide queries.
- Limit batching and aliases.
- Check authorization in every object and field resolver, not only the top-level query.
- Run in production error mode (`NODE_ENV=production` for Apollo).

See the [OWASP GraphQL Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/GraphQL_Cheat_Sheet.html).

*WebSocket flaw:* The server accepts handshakes from any origin, which allows cross-site WebSocket hijacking: a malicious page opens a socket and the browser attaches the victim's cookies. Auth is checked once, at connect.
*Check:* In DevTools, filter the Network tab by WS and inspect the handshake. Connect from another origin with a small script. Check whether permissions are rechecked per message and whether logout closes the socket.
*Fix:* Check the Origin against an allowlist on every handshake, use `wss://` only, authorize each message, and close sockets on logout using a session-to-connection map. See the [OWASP WebSocket Security Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/WebSocket_Security_Cheat_Sheet.html).

*Hosted realtime flaw (Supabase, Firebase):* Generated quick starts leave data readable by anyone.
*Check:* Subscribe from a signed-out client or another tenant's account and see whether rows or messages arrive.
*Fix:* On Supabase, write RLS policies on your tables and on `realtime.messages` for Broadcast and Presence, and turn off "Allow public access" for private channels ([Supabase Realtime Authorization](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/realtime/authorization)). On Firebase, replace the test-mode security rules.

extra_sections.heading: What the reel's diagrams and citation cards show
extra_sections.detail:
The reel shows a small diagram or citation card next to most items:
- **55-56:** a login form with an error line under the password field. It illustrates enumeration, not MFA.
- **57:** a flow labeled "Business Logic Flaw": attacker, then backend, then phone.
- **58:** a lost-update race diagram. Two processes each read a shared balance of 100 and write their own update, and the final value of 110 is marked wrong.
- **60:** an infographic titled "Compromising CI/CD Pipelines", with five panels: Jenkins Pipeline, CI/CD, Credentials, Problem, Attack. The panel text is too small to read.
- **60-61:** a citation card, "Security best practices for authors of GitHub Actions" (GitHub, Fall 2023).
- **62:** the Hacker News comment linked in item 62 above.
- **63:** a citation card, OpenText Community, "Security Fundamentals Part 1: Fail Open vs. Fail Closed". Unconfirmed; see item 63.
- **65:** a diagram labeled "LLM02: Sensitive Information Disclosure". One column is data going into the LLM (PII in prompts, source code in chat, meeting notes). The other is data coming out (training data regurgitation, RAG over-retrieval, system prompt leakage).
- **66:** "Untrusted advice protocol with an information bottleneck". A strong untrusted model may send only a few characters ("del L97") to a weak trusted model, which alone takes action. It comes from a Redwood Research AI-control paper, [Untrusted advice for AI control](https://blog.redwoodresearch.org/p/untrusted-advice-for-ai-control-short). It is research on limiting what a powerful model can pass along, not a product or setting. The reel shows it without attribution.
- **67:** a permission dropdown mockup: "Default permissions / Auto-review / Full access".
- **68:** "Types of Web Storage": Session Storage, Local Storage, Cookies, IndexedDB.
- **69:** a flow from "Safe site" through "Open redirect" to either "correct destination" or "Malicious redirection".
- **70:** an annotated GraphQL query with the labels Query Depth, Query Width, Operations, Field, Directives, Parameters, Aliases, Batches and Fragments. It maps the query's syntax to depth, width, alias and batching attacks.

Items 59 and 64 have no graphic.

extra_sections.heading: Where the rest of the checklist is
extra_sections.detail:
This is Part 4 of a numbered series. Items 1-54 (Parts 1-3) are not published anywhere public. No website, newsletter, GitHub, LinkedIn or X account connected to the creator turned up. The only confirmed home is the [@byarnieverma Instagram profile](https://www.instagram.com/byarnieverma/), so any earlier parts would be reels there.

The caption's offer, "Comment 'risk' for the resource doc", is a comment-to-DM lead magnet, not a link. No public copy of the doc exists. That it is sent by DM automation is an inference from the missing public copy, not something that could be confirmed.

followup.next_action: Run three quick checks on your live app. Send 20 parallel requests to your coupon or checkout endpoint. Grep your workflows for `uses:` lines not pinned to a 40-character SHA. Open DevTools > Application and see whether an auth token is sitting in localStorage.

items.title: 6 Jev Projects to Build Smarter AI Systems
items.hook: Six agent patterns built on Jev, TypeSafe AI's closed classification API: routing, risk gates, triage, loop stops, reranking and guardrails.
items.summary: This carousel pitches six agent patterns built on Jev, a hosted model from TypeSafe AI that returns labels and scores instead of generated text. The patterns are: routing between small and frontier models, allow/block/human-review gates on tool calls, intent triage, continue-or-stop loop decisions, RAG reranking, and policy checks. The slides never name TypeSafe. Jev launched a week before the post as a closed, paid, early-access API. Every pattern can also be built with open-source tools, and several are better done with plain code.

sections.heading: Slide 1: Cover - 6 JEV Projects
sections.detail: Title slide introducing '6 JEV PROJECTS: Build smarter AI systems'. Features a branching diagram with a single source node fanning out into five distinct destination nodes, representing system distribution, orchestration, and decision pathways. Branded with 'LIFE OF ARJAV' and supporting tags 'IDEAS, TOOLS, SYSTEMS, BETTER'.

sections.heading: Slide 2: Model Routing
sections.detail: Jev evaluates incoming task complexity to dynamically route requests between smaller models (for simple tasks) and frontier models (for complex reasoning), saving cost and latency.

sections.heading: Slide 3: Tool-Call Risk Gates
sections.detail: Before executing tool calls, Jev analyzes the tool, arguments, and context to return an Allow, Block, or Human Review decision, preventing hazardous autonomous actions.

sections.heading: Slide 4: Intent + Domain Triage
sections.detail: Incoming requests are pre-classified by Jev into specific categories (e.g., refund_request, bug_report, deployment_issue) before agent reasoning begins.

sections.heading: Slide 5: Loop Decisions
sections.detail: Jev evaluates execution trajectory after each agent step to decide whether to continue the loop or stop, preventing infinite loops and unnecessary token spend.

sections.heading: Slide 6: RAG Reranking
sections.detail: Jev scores retrieved (query, chunk) pairs by relevance to filter and select the top 5 chunks before passing them to the context window.

sections.heading: Slide 7: Guardrails & Policy Checks
sections.detail: Jev converts safety and policy checks into fast classification tasks, blocking unauthorized requests without the overhead of full model generation.

sections.heading: Slide 8: CTA - Get All My Guides
sections.detail: Call-to-action prompting users to comment 'ACCESS' to receive guides, repositories, and templates via DM.

onscreen_text: Jev takes the incoming request and predicts which model should handle it based on task complexity.
Before an agent executes a tool, Jev scores the tool + arguments + current task context and returns a decision.
Jev classifies the request into a fixed set of intents before the main agent starts reasoning.
After every agent step, Jev evaluates the current trajectory and predicts whether another step is likely to be useful.
Jev receives (query, retrieved_chunk) pairs and assigns a relevance score to each chunk.
Jev turns safety checks into fast classification decisions instead of generating a full reasoning response.
Comment ACCESS to get all my guides and repos for free in DMs.

entities.name: Jev
entities.why: The core tool or model framework highlighted across all slides for routing, gating, classifying, reranking, and guardrailing.

entities.name: @lifeofarjav
entities.why: Content creator and source of the guide.

open_questions: Is Jev a specific proprietary library, open-source model, or conceptual framework?
What latency overhead does inserting Jev introduce across each step?

gate.advice: Comment "ACCESS" on the post - the creator sends the link/file back.

followup.answer_html:
Jev is real. It is a closed, hosted classification model from TypeSafe AI, Inc., launched September 15, 2026, one week before this post. The slides never name a maker. The link to TypeSafe rests on three things: the exact name, the timing, and TypeSafe's docs covering the same six uses. That match is strong, but it is an inference.

What Jev is

  • Name on the slides: "JEV" in the cover's all-caps display font and in the caption, and "Jev" on every other slide. The carousel shows no URL, handle, model id or logo.

  • Maker: TypeSafe AI, Inc. See the launch post by founder Diogo Almeida and the Terms of Use. There is also a Wikipedia article.

  • What it does: It does not generate text. It answers typed questions with calibrated probabilities. There are three question types:

    • Choice: pick from a set of options.
    • Score: rate against a 2-10 level rubric.
    • Noul: the probability that a statement is true.

    TypeSafe calls it a "System One Model". This is why every slide frames the job as classify or score.

  • Weights: Closed. There are no public weights, no self-hosting, and no published model size or paper. You customise it per request (state, instructions, criteria), not by fine-tuning. TypeSafe's open code is client-side only: Python and JS SDKs, plus an MIT-licensed agent skill.

  • API: POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone with a Bearer key.

    • Model id jev-1.13.0 is current. jev-latest and jev-preview are aliases.
    • Text input only, up to 64k tokens per request. English is the primary language.
    • Details are in Models and the API reference.

  • Price, as of 2026-09-28: TypeSafe's homepage and models page list $42 per billion input tokens ($0.042 per million). Output tokens are free. TypeSafe has no separate pricing page, so check the models page for the current figure.

  • Access, as of 2026-09-28:

    • The homepage says Jev is in early access. API keys come from console.typesafe.ai, but that page blocked our check, so its signup state is unknown.
    • Third-party write-ups (for example this access guide) report that the waitlist was dropped on Sept 20 and that new signups were paused on Sept 22 because of demand. Some also mention a $5 starting credit.
    • No TypeSafe page we could read confirms the pause or the credit, so treat both as unverified.

  • Docs: docs.typesafe.ai, the quick start and the full docs index. The index has guides on intent routing, confidence-gated routing, re-ranking, classifying RAG passages, guardrails and function calling.

  • Look-alike sites: None of these is run by TypeSafe:

    • jevai.net resells access through referral links at double TypeSafe's input price.
    • jevmodel.org sells its own credits and says it is not affiliated with TypeSafe.
    • jevai.org, jevai.dev and the github.com/jev-ai org are independent.

    TypeSafe's real GitHub org is typesafe-ai. JevRouter is a genuine MIT-licensed community client that calls TypeSafe's API, but TypeSafe does not make it.

  • The creator's own material: Comment "ACCESS" on the post and the creator sends guides and repos by DM. That is the only way to get them. The creator's site does not mention Jev.

Building the six patterns

With Jev, each pattern is one API call that returns a label or a score. Its selling points are speed and a low input price. The tradeoff is that it is a closed, early-access API. Every pattern can also be built without Jev.

  1. Model routing (small vs frontier model)

    • Jev: ask a Choice question with two options.
    • Open source: RouteLLM (Apache 2.0) uses trained routers. It reports up to 85% cost savings while keeping 95% of GPT-4 quality on MT-Bench. Its last commit was in August 2024, so treat it as reference code. semantic-router (MIT) routes by similarity to example phrases and can run fully locally.
    • Paid: Not Diamond is a hosted router at $0.05 per million tokens routed, as of 2026-09-28. Its docs cite 100-150 ms of added latency.
    • Plain code: if your traffic is not very varied, a rule on input length or keywords is enough. Be careful with cascades (try the small model first, escalate on failure). When most requests are hard, a cascade can cost more than always calling the frontier model.

  2. Tool-call risk gates (allow / block / human review)

    • Start with plain code: an allowlist of tool names, a JSON Schema check on arguments, and a human-approval step. The OpenAI Agents SDK lets you mark a tool as needing approval. The run then pauses until you approve or reject the call (see the approvals guide). It is free and open source. Its docs warn that approval is not a sandbox, so your executor still has to enforce real permissions.
    • Rules engine: Open Policy Agent (Apache 2.0, free) handles rules you can write down, such as "block any delete tool above a set amount".
    • Model-based, for cases rules cannot cover: Meta's LlamaFirewall is open source, though its page does not state a license or latency figure. A three-option Jev Choice also fits here.
    • Caution: a gate that only reads the tool name and arguments can be fooled by instructions injected through earlier tool output. Scan tool output before it goes back into context.

  3. Intent and domain triage

    • Jev: ask a Choice question over your fixed label set.
    • Open source, no training: semantic-router with a few example phrases per intent. It needs one embedding call and no text generation. A local encoder is free. A hosted one costs very little: text-embedding-3-small is $0.02 per million tokens as of 2026-09-28.
    • Open source, once you have labelled data: SetFit (Apache 2.0) fine-tunes a small classifier from as few as 8 examples per class and runs on a CPU.
    • Framework: NeMo Guardrails topical rails map each message to a fixed intent before choosing what to do next.

  4. Loop decisions (continue or stop)

    • This is mostly plain code.
    • Hard cap on steps: LangGraph's recursion_limit, or max_turns in the OpenAI Agents SDK, which raises MaxTurnsExceeded when hit. CrewAI has max_iter. All are open source and free.
    • Early stop: compare the last few steps and stop when nothing is changing (same output, a repeated error, a metric that is not moving). Base the stop on an outside signal, such as tests passing, not on the agent's own view of whether it is done.
    • A learned stop model (a Jev Noul question or your own classifier) only pays off once your logs show the simple rules stopping too early or too late. No ready-made product for this was found.

  5. RAG reranking

    • Jev: ask a Score question for each (query, chunk) pair. TypeSafe's docs have guides on re-ranking and on classifying RAG passages.
    • Open weights, self-hosted and free to run:
      • BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3: Apache 2.0, 0.6B parameters, multilingual. LangChain's cross-encoder guide calls it a strong default and shows how to plug it in.
      • mxbai-rerank-large-v2: Apache 2.0, 1.5B parameters.
      • jina-reranker-v2-base-multilingual: licensed CC-BY-NC-4.0, so commercial self-hosting needs a separate license from Jina.
    • Hosted and paid:
      • Voyage: rerank-2.5 is $0.05 and rerank-2.5-lite $0.02 per million tokens, as of 2026-09-28.
      • Cohere Rerank: closed. Its pricing page shows no self-serve per-search price.
      • Jina Reranker API: free tier of 100 requests per minute.
    • Start with bge-reranker-v2-m3.

  6. Guardrails and policy checks

    • Free hosted: the OpenAI Moderation API is free and covers 13 harm categories. It returns a flagged value plus per-category scores.
    • Open weights: Llama Guard 3 8B (Llama 3.1 Community License) covers 14 hazard categories in 8 languages.
    • Open-source frameworks: NeMo Guardrails and Guardrails AI, both Apache 2.0.
    • Paid, metered: AWS Bedrock Guardrails. Content filters and denied topics cost $0.15 per 1,000 text units, word filters are free, and blocked requests are not charged, as of 2026-09-28.
    • Jev: one Choice or Noul question per policy.
    • The caution from pattern 2 applies here too. These tools check user input and final output, not tool output in the middle of an agent loop.

items.title: Get Certified with Anthropic's Claude Certified Architect Foundations Exam
items.hook: Anthropic's $125 Claude architect exam is real, but you need a partner-company email to register, and employers have no track record with it yet.
items.summary: Claude Certified Architect - Foundations (CCAR-F) is Anthropic's official exam, launched March 2026 and delivered by Pearson VUE: 60 questions, 120 minutes, $125 per attempt, 720/1000 to pass, valid 12 months. Registration needs a work email at a Claude Partner Network company. The exam tests Claude Code, the Agent SDK, MCP, structured output and context management, not model selection or cost as the reel says. The four free prep courses are live and open to anyone. The reel's Deloitte line refers to a separate, earlier internal Deloitte training program.

sections.heading: Overview and Industry Adoption
sections.detail: Deloitte paid thousands of employees to get certified through Anthropic's official certification program, which is accessible to anyone.

sections.heading: Credential Details
sections.detail: Named 'Claude Certified Architect – Foundations', this certification proves competence in architecting Claude solutions, choosing models, designing agentic versus single-shot architectures, and managing costs and evaluations.

sections.heading: Free Preparation Courses
sections.detail: Anthropic Academy offers free preparatory courses: AI Fluency: Framework & Foundations (Level 100), Claude 101 (Level 100), Building with the Claude API (Level 100-200), and Claude with Amazon Bedrock (Level 100-200).

sections.heading: Exam Format and Cost
sections.detail: The exam consists of 60 multiple-choice questions with a 120-minute time limit (~135-minute seat time) and costs $125 USD.

sections.heading: Registration
sections.detail: Candidates can sign up and access materials at anthropic-partners.skilljar.com/claude-certified-architect-foundations-certification.

onscreen_text: Validates that you can scope and design Claude-based solutions: selecting the right model and deployment platform, framing agentic versus single-shot architectures, and accounting for evaluation, cost, and responsible deployment from day one.
These free courses on the Anthropic Academy cover the domains above. Most candidates complete them in order, then register.
Learn to collaborate with AI systems effectively, efficiently, ethically, and safely.
Use Claude for everyday work tasks, understand core features, and explore resources for more advanced learning.
Working with Anthropic models using the Claude API — from authentication, prompt engineering, and evaluations through tool use, RAG, agents, and production patterns.
Working with Anthropic models through Amazon Bedrock — setup and foundational concepts through tool use, RAG, agents, and production patterns.
